title: HiMEM: Hippocampus-Inspired Memory Consolidation, Pruning, and Composition for Vision-Language-Action Models in 3D Scenes
summary: Memory plays a crucial role in long-horizon task execution and cross-task generalization for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models operating in complex 3D scenes. However, existing VLA memory mechanisms suffer from memory noise, particularly in complex 3D scenes, as stored episodic memories contain extensive redundant details about scene layouts, object configurations, and robot-specific states, which obscure generalizable manipulation principles and hinder cross-task transfer. To address this challenge, we first introduce a hippocampus-inspired memory consolidation mechanism that synthesizes extensive episodic experiences into a compact set of essential semantic memories, enabling VLA models to derive generalizable principles from practical experience. Second, we propose an episodic memory pruning mechanism that removes redundant episodic memories whose contents are captured by consolidated semantic memories, thereby increasing effective memory capacity and improving long-horizon task execution. Finally, to handle complex task scenarios, we develop a flexible memory composition mechanism that jointly leverages multiple episodic and semantic memories to enhance cross-scenario generalization. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus demonstrate the effectiveness of HiMEM across different VLA backbones, improving the average success rate of pi_0 from 91.88% to 98.20% on LIBERO.

title: Challenges, Opportunities, and Misconceptions in Neurosymbolic AI
summary: We examine opportunities for neurosymbolic AI alongside increasingly powerful neural models, particularly with regards to efficiency, safety and interpretability. We identify two major challenges: ensuring semantic alignment between neural and symbolic components, and managing the computational cost of symbolic inference and learning. We discuss representative methodological approaches to these challenges and address several common misconceptions concerning differentiability, independence assumptions, and scalability. This paper synthesizes perspectives developed through discussions in the Neurosymbolic Programming and Reasoning (NPR) working group at the 2026 CNRS workshop Neurosymbolic Methods and Their Applications in Data Science, rather than providing an exhaustive survey.

title: SafeOrchestrate: Runtime Checked Intent-Driven Orchestration for Cyber-Physical Systems
summary: Modern cyber physical systems (CPS) integrate heterogeneous sensors, actuators, controllers, and services, composed at runtime rather than at design time. Orchestrating such systems through natural language (NL) is attractive, but unconstrained large language model (LLM) tool use is risky because actions must respect device capabilities, runtime state, and safety constraints. We present Safe Orchestrate, a reference architecture for runtime checked, intent driven CPS orchestration. Given an NL intent, it derives atomic goals, generates a runtime checkable specification for each, grounds the specifications to device affordances, and verifies every candidate action against runtime state and safety constraints before execution. In a Web of Things (WoT) instantiation, the architecture produces Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) style specifications from the NL intent, grounds them to Thing Description (TD) affordances exposed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), and checks candidate actions against satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) backed guardrails. We evaluate this instantiation on simulated smart home, greenhouse, and industrial automation tasks against a direct LLM to MCP baseline. Safe Orchestrate maintains 100% required action accuracy on every task and 100% MCP Execution Similarity (MCP ES) on all but one, where MCP ES is 92%. By contrast, the baseline degrades on multi device, event triggered, and ordered tasks, with MCP ES falling to 13%. These results suggest that combining LLM based specification generation with role aware grounding and runtime constraint checking improves reliability for open CPS orchestration without enriched TD annotations or planning domain expertise.

title: Anchored Iterative Decoding of Reed-Solomon Product Codes for High-Rate Magnetic Tape Storage
summary: We present a decoding algorithm for a Reed--Solomon product code targeted at the demanding reliability requirements of modern magnetic tape storage. For a code $RS(256, 224)\times RS(175, 173)$ in a BSC we achieve post-decoding bit error rate (BER) of $10^{-20}$ at $\approx 5.3\times 10^{-3}$ raw BER while maintaining the common requirement to detect and correct 4 out of 32 dead tracks. We resolve two common problems of miscorrections and stall patterns that arise under such a high raw BER via simplified versions of anchor decoding and binary image analysis. The highest efficiency is achieved by performing an unlimited iterative decoder, which performs decoding iterations until no changes are made. We give an empirical analysis of the average number of iterations: below the raw BER of $5\times 10^{-3}$, four half-iterations are performed on average while improving substantially over a decoder that always performs 4 half-iterations. We provide a CPU implementation achieving 100-200 megabytes/s single-core throughput on a regular laptop and a design of a potential hybrid FPGA-CPU implementation of our decoder.

title: Mitigating Covariate Shift in Behavioral Cloning via Robust Stationary Distribution Correction
summary: We consider offline imitation learning (IL), which aims to train an agent to imitate from the dataset of expert demonstrations without online interaction with the environment. Behavioral Cloning (BC) has been a simple yet effective approach to offline IL, but it is also well-known to be vulnerable to the covariate shift resulting from the mismatch between the state distributions induced by the learned policy and the expert policy. Moreover, as often occurs in practice, when expert datasets are collected from an arbitrary state distribution instead of a stationary one, these shifts become more pronounced, potentially leading to substantial failures in existing IL methods. Specifically, we focus on covariate shift resulting from arbitrary state data distributions, such as biased data collection or incomplete trajectories, rather than shifts induced by changes in dynamics or noisy expert actions. In this paper, to mitigate the effect of the covariate shifts in BC, we propose DrilDICE, which utilizes a distributionally robust BC objective by employing a stationary distribution correction ratio estimation (DICE) to derive a feasible solution. We evaluate the effectiveness of our method through an extensive set of experiments covering diverse covariate shift scenarios. The results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach in improving the robustness against the shifts, outperforming existing offline IL methods in such scenarios.

title: Enabling Privacy-Preserving Natural Language Access to Industrial Smart Meter Data
summary: Energy management officers and grid operators increasingly rely on smart meter data for anomaly detection, performance monitoring, and strategic decision-making. However, extracting actionable insights from large-scale, heterogeneous telemetry databases requires advanced SQL and data engineering expertise, creating a critical bottleneck for non-technical personnel. Furthermore, the strict data privacy regulations and security constraints inherent to critical energy infrastructure often prohibit the routing of sensitive consumer data through cloud-based Large Language Models (LLMs). To address these challenges, we present OpenMeter, a schema-agnostic Multi-Agent System (MAS) designed to translate natural language queries into executable code and human-readable insights. This architecture lowers the technical barrier for day-to-day utility operations by empowering non-expert personnel to interact with complex databases through intuitive natural language dialogue, transforming raw telemetry into a highly valuable tool for routine grid workflows and strategic decisions. Multi-scenario ablation studies over this environment demonstrate that full multi-agent orchestration shows its largest observed accuracy gains on resource-constrained local hardware (+6.1 pp EX-R over the strongest single-agent configuration); at frontier scale, individual components retain value but should be enabled selectively, indicating that the cost of full orchestration is justified specifically where privacy demands local execution.

title: Calibrated Uncertainty Quantification on TDC ADMET: What Can Be Resolved Across 22 Datasets?
comments: 33 pages. Preprint of a paper accepted for poster presentation at the AIDaR Workshop at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET) models often rely on small, heterogeneous datasets, yet their predictions may determine which compounds proceed to experimental testing. Useful evaluations must therefore assess both predictive performance and the quality of reported probabilities or intervals. We ask which common uncertainty-quantification methods perform best on the 22 Therapeutics Data Commons (TDC) ADMET datasets and what this benchmark can resolve. We compare eleven calibrated pipelines using nested five-fold cross-validation across ten chemical partitions and five model seeds. Ensemble Monte Carlo (MC) dropout has the best average rank for TDC performance, Brier score, and 90% interval score. For TDC performance, however, it is not separated from the other ensemble pipelines; for Brier and interval score, LightGBM is also not ruled out as best. LightGBM wins more individual datasets than any other method for TDC performance and Brier score, but performs poorly on several endpoints. Smaller evaluations can identify a different leader and often fail to recover the broader comparison. These results make LightGBM and an ensemble neural model complementary baselines. Comparative claims should be checked across multiple chemical partitions using statistical analyses matched to the question being asked.
comment: 33 pages. Preprint of a paper accepted for poster presentation at the AIDaR Workshop at NeurIPS 2026

title: Pairwise Reconnection for Cost-Distance Steiner Trees
summary:
The Uniform Cost-Distance Steiner Tree Problem asks for a rooted tree that minimizes the connection cost plus a weighted sum of root-to-terminal distances. We develop an algorithm that constructs two candidate trees: one based on direct connections to the root and another that pairs selected vertices and connects each pair to the root. The algorithm selects the tree with the smaller objective value. The resulting randomized algorithm achieves expected approximation factors of $1.698$ in the spanning case and $2.041$ in the general case, and it can be derandomized in polynomial time. The pairwise matching analysis charges part of the augmentation cost directly to the connection and delay costs of an optimal solution, rather than only to the separated lower bound used in previous analyses. This allows the $1.698$ factor to fall below the maximum multiplicative gap of $1+1/\sqrt{2}$ between the optimum value and that lower bound.
  We give instance families with approximation-ratio lower bounds approaching $1+1/\sqrt{2}$ for cut-and-reconnect algorithms that start from a minimum spanning tree and $3/2$ for the present algorithm. Finally, we show that the Uniform Cost-Distance Steiner Tree Problem and the Steiner-tree version of the Cable-Trench Problem are approximation equivalent up to an arbitrarily small additive loss.

title: Cutpurse: Decomposing Explanation-Guided Model Extraction on Tabular Data
summary:
Explanation APIs are often treated as increasing model-extraction risk, but an end-to-end attack comparison cannot show whether an explanation reveals model-specific information or merely supplies a convenient next-query coordinate. We study this distinction for explanation-guided extraction of tabular classifiers. We separate an explanation into an attribution channel, which ranks influential features, and a coordinate channel, which supplies candidate feature values for perturbing those features. We then test whether the useful bin edges are privileged to the service or reproducible from the adversary's own data.
  Across six datasets and five target families, using attribution rankings to choose which features to perturb provides no systematic extraction advantage. Lime's discretization bin edges can improve fidelity by up to 41 percentage points on continuous features, but those edges are quantiles of the explainer's background data rather than properties of the target model. In controlled comparisons, an attacker-side grid reproduces the useful bin-edge gains without querying an explanation API. We use these findings to derive Cutpurse, which combines a self-computed grid with diverse query generation and boundary search. Against a service that withholds bin edges, Cutpurse improves fidelity by 16.3 percentage points on continuous-feature targets. It also exceeds the undefended published attack by 7.0 percentage points. Thus, withholding default Lime bin edges alone does not prevent effective extraction under the in-domain auxiliary-input, probability-output, and same-family surrogate assumptions studied here. Our results concern default Lime and Shap configurations for tabular classifiers. They do not establish the same conclusion for other explainers, target classes, or data-free attackers.

title: Can LLMs Debug Robots by Editing Their Weights?
summary: A language model can repair a robot policy's lexical instruction grounding by editing just 65 token-embedding rows. We bring weight-space programming to robot foundation policies: GPT-6 Astra reads weights and uses a CPU workspace and budgeted simulator feedback, without gradient updates or new demonstrations. Three independent sessions on $π_{0.5}$ all improve success on 765 held-out paraphrases; the best raises success from 86.3\% to 92.0\% (48 repairs, four regressions; exact paired $p=1.31\times10^{-10}$). Among the 335 instructions containing edited tokens, success rises from 74.3\% to 87.5\%; the other 430 episodes have zero outcome changes. Matched random-direction edits do not help. Full replacement using the editor's own lexicon explains much of the gain but produces more regressions; its direct difference from the editor is not significant at 0.05. Across 13 further robot sessions, the editor declines 12 candidates; the sole retained edit does not show a significant held-out gain. Separately, benchmark metadata lowers FastWAM success from 70.0\% to 48.6\%, while the evaluated VLA's aggregate rate is unchanged. The evidence supports precise lexical repair, not general acquisition of missing robot capabilities.

title: KineCouple: Substrate-conditioned residual readout for enzyme kinetic prediction
summary: Accurate prediction of enzyme kinetic parameters can support enzyme engineering and metabolic modeling by complementing experimental characterization. Existing prediction methods often pool residue-level protein features before combining them with substrate features. Such substrate-independent pooling cannot adapt residue weighting to the substrate during aggregation, potentially diluting information relevant to a specific enzyme-substrate pair. Since the contributions of individual residues to catalysis can depend on the substrate, substrate-conditioned aggregation offers a way to emphasize residue features relevant to the prediction. We introduce KineCouple, which uses substrate queries and residue-level keys and values in cross-attention, allowing the substrate to guide residue selection before aggregation. The model preserves the global protein representation and adds a gated correction defined as the difference between the conditioned readout and a uniform readout. ProtT5 and MolT5 remain frozen, and separate models predict kcat and Km on a logarithmic scale. In pooled out-of-fold predictions on the CataPro benchmarks, KineCouple reduces kcat RMSE from 1.333 to 1.330 and increases PCC from 0.492 to 0.496 relative to reproduced CataPro. For Km, RMSE decreases from 0.998 to 0.997 and PCC increases from 0.633 to 0.634. Spearman correlation also improves for both tasks.

title: SPSC: Zero-Shot Cross-Subject EEG-to-Image Reconstruction via Semantic Preservation and Subspace Calibration
summary: Pretrained vision-language models and diffusion generators have driven rapid progress in brain-to-image generation, while EEG-based reconstruction is still constrained by low signal-to-noise ratio and cross-subject semantic shifts. Zero-shot cross-subject reconstruction poses even greater challenges: EEG semantic embeddings learned from source subjects deviate from the manifold of image embeddings of the unseen target subject, particularly when neither target labels nor target image embeddings are available. To address this issue, we introduce the Semantic Preservation and Subspace Calibration (SPSC) framework, which first uses Object Mask Contrastive Regularization (OMCR) with object identity for backend training, and then constructs Subspace Candidate Gate (SCG) to achieve label-free semantic correction for target subjects during inference. Specifically, OMCR regularizes the conditioning space with object-level positive samples to preserve object-level feature neighborhoods within the reconstruction prior and low-level branch, while SCG exploits training image prototypes and batch statistics of unlabeled target EEG to select candidates for each task within subspaces of image prototypes. Under the leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) setting across ten subjects on the THINGS-EEG dataset, SPSC improves the cross-subject reconstruction from 0.552 to 0.713 on CLIP and from 0.612 to 0.745 on Alex.5. These significant gains indicate that the semantically calibrated conditions can better support generation for the target subjects under label-free inference.

title: Exploring Weight-Space Programming: Capabilities, Generalization, and Limitations
summary:
Weight-Space Programming (WSP) enables reasoning agents to directly inspect and modify neural network parameters, offering an alternative to gradient-based model adaptation. However, its capabilities, cross-task generalization, and practical limitations remain insufficiently understood. We systematically investigate WSP through 16 editing trajectories across seven benchmarks and two model scales (Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-9B). Our findings reveal three key insights. First, WSP can achieve substantial performance gains through highly localized interventions. On full held-out evaluations, accuracy improves by up to 29.45, 4.42, 36.72, and 17.11 percentage points on MATH-500, GPQA Diamond, IFEval, and SciBench, respectively. Notably, modifying only 1,023 parameters yields a 29.45-point improvement. Second, WSP exhibits promising but uneven cross-task generalization. A Math-edited checkpoint improves GPQA Diamond, IFEval, and SciBench by 3.03, 12.18, and 20.10 points, respectively, without further editing, while leaving SciCode performance unchanged. Third, effective editing remains challenging and inconsistent. Outcomes vary substantially across trajectories, and six of the 16 trajectories retain the original weights when candidate improvements cannot be reliably validated. Together, these results highlight WSP's potential for highly localized model adaptation while revealing important challenges in intervention discovery, reliability, and cross-task transfer.
  Homepage: https://wsp-scope.github.io/ GitHub: https://github.com/WSP-Scope/WSP-Scope-Project

title: Universal Decoding for Gaussian MIMO-ISI: Spherical Ensembles and Symmetric Neighborhoods
summary: We construct a universal decoder for cyclic Gaussian multiple-input multiple-output channels with intersymbol interference and unknown channel taps and spatial noise covariance. Codewords are drawn independently and uniformly from a sphere of fixed total energy. Under stated bounds on frequency variation, the decoder attains the ensemble-average error exponent of informed maximum-likelihood decoding for fixed channels and channels with growing memory. We approximate the frequency response by a constant matrix within each frequency block. For this auxiliary channel, every matched log-likelihood is affine in a common sufficient statistic. At fixed received output, we compute the statistic density of an independent competitor. The decoder selects the candidate with the smallest statistic density, equivalently minimizing a weighted sum of residual log-determinants. The density and its support volume give an upper bound on the universal competitor probability. Affinity ensures that at least half of a suitable symmetric neighborhood of the transmitted statistic has matched likelihood no smaller than that of the transmitted word. Integrating a density lower bound over this half gives the matched competitor bound. These bounds establish equality of error exponents, which a Gaussian channel comparison transfers to the original channel. The same decoder attains the matched exponent for independent frequency blocks with prescribed energies satisfying the stated conditions. For energies proportional to block length, an additional gain condition ensures that this exponent is at least that of the total-energy spherical ensemble.

title: Against All Likelihood
summary: Maximum likelihood is the dominant training principle for large language models, yet likelihood is neither necessary nor sufficient for truth. Unlikely events happen every day, and frequently repeated statements can be false. Drawing on a philosophical tradition that ties objectivity to invariance rather than probability (from Nozick's account of objective facts and Wigner's principles of invariance to the structural realism of Poincaré and Cassirer), we argue that the truth of a statement should be judged not by its probability under a single distribution, but by its invariance across relevant transformations of the environment. We connect this view to machine learning literature on out-of-distribution generalization and invariant learning, sketch how invariance could be tested at inference time with language models, and discuss implications for continual learning.

title: A Bridge from Paste to Place: Physics-Guided One-Step Image Composition via Object-Scene Interaction
summary: Realistic image composition must make a pasted object appear naturally present in a scene while preserving the fine details of both foreground and background. Reference-based insertion methods can change object pose and appearance, while foreground harmonization methods and shadow-specific synthesis methods each address only part of this task. An efficient, unified solution to this task remains an open challenge. We introduce Paste2Place, an end-to-end, physics-guided flow-based model that learns a direct, one-step latent bridge from pasted inputs to realistic composites, guided by explicit albedo-shading-residual decomposition and recomposition within the model. To support model training and evaluation, we develop a Blender rendering and validation pipeline to generate paired composites with physical annotations, and construct real-scene pairs from open-source object-removal data. This effort yields 86,273 training pairs and a 1,500-example benchmark. Extensive qualitative and quantitative experiments demonstrate that Paste2Place achieves substantial advantages in image composition quality and inference speed. Overall, our work provides a clear task definition and an effective solution for image composition, and fills a gap in large-scale, high-quality datasets and benchmarks for training and evaluating image composition.

title: k-Volume: a Unified Active Learning Strategy
summary: In the classification context where revealing the label of a sample is costly, we propose a new Active Learning (AL) strategy named k-Volume (kVol). It randomly selects a sample to be labeled according to the volume of the smallest ball containing its k nearest neighbors. kVol is highly versatile: it can be applied either in the input space or in the output space, and it enjoys the desirable properties of the three main families of AL strategies: density, diversity, and (when performed in the output space) uncertainty. From a theoretical perspective, we establish that kVol is asymptotically equivalent to uniform sampling over the support of the (input or output) data distribution. Based on experiments on various synthetic and real-life tabular datasets and images, we observe that kVol is surprisingly stable: whatever the classifier or the experimental setup, it still lies among the best AL strategies unlike other competitors that fail dramatically. In particular, kVol outperforms state-of-the-art competitors such as CoreSet, TypiClust or Uncertainty on several real-life datasets, at a low computational cost.

title: Precedence Constraint Scheduling on a Fixed Number of Machines
summary:
We give a deterministic exact algorithm for $P_m\mid\mathrm{prec},p_j=1\mid C_{\max}$ for every fixed $m\ge3$. The algorithm constructs an optimum schedule in $$
  O(L)+m^{O(m^2)}\, n^{6m^2+13m+1} \, {\log n} $$ elementary RAM operations, where $n \ge 2$ is the number of jobs and $L$ is the binary input length. Its word size is $O(m^2 \log n)$ bits. An implementation with a fixed number of tapes uses $O(L)+m^{O(m^2)} \, n^{12m^2+26m+2} \, \log^3 n$ steps. For three machines the respective polynomial degrees are $94$ and $188$, apart from the displayed logarithmic factors.

title: Sensed but Not Told: Hidden Physiological Adaptation Shapes LLM Persuasion
summary: Wearable sensors, including those embedded in VR headsets, can provide LLM-based chatbots with physiological signals that users do not explicitly communicate. We tested whether such hidden input changes persuasion. In a $2\times2$ within-subjects study ($N=24$), a chatbot argued against participants' self-selected opinions with or without turn-level heart-rate and pupil-diameter features; sensing was disclosed halfway through the study. Before disclosure, sensing increased perceived persuasiveness by 1.42 points. Across the study, sensing was associated with a 0.57-point greater shift toward the chatbot's position and 3.20 times the odds of any movement toward it. Persuasiveness ratings were lower after disclosure, although disclosure was confounded with session order. Dialogue logs suggested a more declarative interaction style when sensing was on: chatbot replies contained question marks less often, and conversations contained fewer turns. These findings motivate making biosignal-driven adaptation inspectable and providing a genuinely non-sensed mode.

title: Tracybot: Preserving Developer Intent by Tracing Agent-Generated Code to Prompts
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are now widely used in software development, and LLM-based coding agents are given increasing autonomy. With coding agents, many design decisions are made in the conversation between the developer and the agent. Typically, the developer starts a conversation with an agent and states their intent, the agent proposes options if needed, and the developer plans the change accordingly. Then, the resulting code is committed. However, in such scenarios, the decisions and the intent behind the changes remain in the conversation, with no link to the code they produced. In this paper, we present Tracybot, an open-source tool that integrates with VS Code, Git, and coding agents to keep track of relevant conversations in an LLM-assisted development process. Tracybot captures each change as a Tasklet which consists of optional planning prompts used to plan a change, together with a build prompt that produces it. Tracybot has two main features: (i) it maps line-level code changes made by coding agents to the Tasklets that produced them, and (ii) it allows the developer to export a Tasklet as a decision record when needed, for example when the decision concerns the architecture of the project. We developed the tool over two iterations of a design science study, while focusing the evaluation on the usability and user-friendliness of the tool. In a focus group (7 participants) and a survey (24 participants), we found that Tracybot was perceived as useful for activities like code review, and most participants found our Tasklet design and presentation to be a clear way to represent the developer's intent. Tool: https://github.com/TracyTeam/tracybot. Video: https://youtu.be/Vg_a1F5eO04.

title: Travel Cost Calibration for Multi-Agent Target Assignment and Pathfinding
summary: Target assignment and pathfinding (TAPF) is an appealing extension of classical multi-agent pathfinding (MAPF): each agent has a set of targets, and the planner must both assign a target to each agent and plan collision-free paths for them. A trivial approach is to compute an assignment that minimizes the total single-agent shortest-path distance over agent--target pairs, and then solve the resulting MAPF instance. However, this approach falls short because the shortest-path distance remains a proxy that ignores interference among agents. Assigning targets based on the costs agents actually pay, which depend on how every other agent is assigned and routed, would yield a better final outcome. To this end, we propose an iterative TAPF method that improves target assignments by calibrating travel cost estimates from fast, suboptimal MAPF feedback. Experiments show that our method produces solutions close to optimal on small instances and outperforms existing planners in solution quality on larger ones.

title: Causal graph fusion across incomplete cohorts and causal steering of tabular foundation models
summary: Clinical data are split across incomplete cohorts with partially overlapping variables. Causal discovery under missing data and multi-source integration have developed separately, and tabular foundation models cannot take a causal graph without retraining. We make two contributions. First, causal graph fusion learns a partial ancestral graph on the shared variables, fuses it into each cohort's graph under temporal background knowledge and lets Markov blankets guide re-imputation, so missing data are handled inside discovery. Second, causal attention steering compiles the learned graph into the attention of a frozen tabular foundation model at inference. Against known ground truth, fusion dominates pooled and per-cohort baselines in every missingness and heterogeneity condition tested (p<0.001), and steering improves discrimination under distribution shift (p<10^{-5}), a gain that a random graph does not produce. In two spinal cord injury cohorts, fusion orients age, albumin and hemoglobin as ancestors of length of stay, a set no single cohort orients in full, and yields compact, temporally ordered predictor sets that match or exceed automatic feature selection on four of five outcomes.

title: PhyCAD: Physics-Aware Text-to-CAD Generation via Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning
summary: Language-driven computer-aided design (CAD) generation enables the creation of editable parametric models from text, yet geometric correctness alone does not ensure physical feasibility. We present PhyCAD, a framework for physics-aware Text-to-CAD generation that trains language models to produce executable CadQuery programs under geometric and physical constraints. To support this setting, we construct a Text-to-CAD dataset that links parametric CAD models with geometric specifications, loading conditions, and physical constraints. We further develop an automated CAD--CAE verifier that combines program execution, geometric checks, and finite element analysis to provide feedback for model training. A key learning challenge is to prioritize joint satisfaction of geometric and physical constraints while retaining informative feedback on partial progress. A flat aggregation of heterogeneous rewards can obscure this priority, allowing improvements in individual criteria to compensate for unmet design requirements. We therefore introduce a Hierarchical Balanced Advantage for Group Relative Policy Optimization, grouping candidates into levels according to their verification status and combining between-level progress with objective-wise peer ranking within each level. This formulation preserves cross-level priority in the training signal while providing fine-grained feedback for satisfying constraints and improving feasible designs. Experiments across multiple language models show that PhyCAD consistently improves joint geometric and physical constraint satisfaction. These results demonstrate the value of verifiable engineering feedback for advancing language-driven CAD generation beyond geometric reconstruction toward physics-aware design.

title: A Spiking Neural Model of the Mental Lexicon: Representations, Similarity Structure, and Associative Retrieval in Perception and Production
comments: 28 pages, 3 figures; code, lexical data and recorded simulations available on GitHub; ancillary figure-generation scripts and provenance documentation
summary: A neural account of lexical access requires an explicit distinction between the structure of lexical representations, the associations linking representational levels, and the activity generated during retrieval. This paper specifies a spiking neural implementation of the mental lexicon within the Neural Engineering Framework and Semantic Pointer Architecture. Conceptual and phonological form representations are constructed recursively from relational graphs, whereas lemma representations provide independent lexical identities. The implementation contains 613 lexical entries and supports two directed processing pathways: perception maps a phonological form to its associated concept via a lemma, whereas production maps a concept to its associated phonological form via a lemma. Each pathway combines two associative-memory variants, winner-take-all (WTA) selection (competition) and thresholded transfer, and uses 199,400 leaky integrate-and-fire neurons. We formalize within-level similarity, cross-level associative retrieval, and the interpretation of decoded activity. Simulations show successful retrieval of eight selected words from the lexicon in both processing directions, with retrieval evaluated against all 613 lexical entries. These simulations use complete phonological forms as input for perception and complete concepts as input for production, illustrating lexical retrieval through the corresponding processing pathways. This paper provides a transparent description of lexical representations and neural retrieval mechanisms, supported by accessible code, lexical data, and online simulation documentation.
comment: 28 pages, 3 figures; code, lexical data and recorded simulations available on GitHub; ancillary figure-generation scripts and provenance documentation

title: Uniqueness-Aware Feature Engineering for Representing Humans in Algorithmic Decision Making
summary: Fairness analyses of algorithmic decision systems typically treat the feature representation of individuals as an a priori fixed input. How well a feature representation captures what is actually decision-relevant for different people and their unique backgrounds, however, is typically left unexamined. We address this gap by modeling feature engineering as a stochastic selection process over the pooled characteristics as candidate features for a finite training population. Based on this model, we develop a new framework for uniqueness-aware feature engineering which operates in two layers. The first layer measures population heterogeneity using a multivariate hypergeometric model of feature prevalence. It shows how well an individual is represented by any given input representation and which individual of the population is "least represented" compared to their personal, reference characteristics. The second layer acts on this assessment using set-similarity measures to search for an optimum between representational fit of the population and predictive accuracy. Without assuming prior knowledge about unseen individuals, our framework grants represented humans agency over what counts as decision-relevant in their case, gives deploying institutions accountability through a publishable representation fit report, and provides each person subject to a decision transparency about their personal representation fit. We operationalize our framework as a six-step pipeline and show a proof-of-principle using synthetic data. Our approach offers a blueprint for making algorithmic decision systems accountable for how well they represent individuals during development and in production.

title: ROAM: Retrieval-Augmented Optimization for Feasible Multi-Day Itinerary Planning
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can draft plausible travel itineraries, but the plans they produce are frequently infeasible: attractions are grouped into days without regard for geography, opening hours are ignored, and a single generation pass cannot reliably organize a multi-day trip. We present ROAM, a retrieval-augmented agentic framework for spontaneous multi-day itinerary planning that couples semantic preference retrieval with explicit spatiotemporal optimization. ROAM embeds the natural-language request, retrieves a compact candidate set from a curated point-of-interest (POI) database, partitions candidates into day groups through maximal-clique analysis and K-means, orders each day with a quality-biased simulated-annealing TSP solver, and repairs hard opening-hour violations with greedy exchange. A spatiotemporal retrieval layer injects weather forecasts, real road distances and POI operating hours into the prompt, after which the LLM renders a structured, map-ready itinerary; an interactive ReAct-style replanning agent then supports natural-language edits while re-checking feasibility. Across four Chinese cities and 510 POIs, ROAM produces 27.5 POIs per three-day plan versus 19.3 for a bare LLM and 17.0 for a retrieval-only baseline (+42% and +62%), while reducing route dispersion from 2,101 to 677 (3.1x). Ablations show that spatial optimization is the dominant driver of route efficiency and that hard time-window repair prevents roughly 30% of attractions from violating operating hours.

title: Nothing Is Shared Until You Synchronise: Reinterpreting Java for Data-Race Freedom
summary:
In mainstream shared-memory languages, programmers use synchronisation mechanisms such as locks to isolate shared data accesses across threads to avoid data races. Yet synchronisation enforces only a temporal ordering, while shared memory still communicates updates between threads at every ordinary read and write. To achieve isolation, programmers therefore need to understand the connection between ordering and communication, and to apply synchronisation correctly and consistently, while compilers and hardware optimise assuming they have. When programmers synchronise incorrectly, they lose isolation, and the semantics of their programs change without notice.
  We propose Sync-as-Share, a memory model built on isolation and communication rather than on the ordering of accesses to shared memory. We start from thread isolation, where each thread reads and writes a private view of memory, and reinterpret programs' existing synchronisation actions to also communicate updates explicitly. As nothing is communicated outside synchronisation actions, data races become impossible by construction. Instead, conflicting updates are detected at synchronisation points. Viewing synchronisation as explicit communication exposes the design decisions of what should be communicated, to whom, and what counts as a conflict. We propose two communication topologies with different trade-offs. We instantiate Sync-as-Share for Java by making the synchronisation actions already defined by its memory model the only points at which threads communicate, so Java programs can adopt Sync-as-Share unmodified. We formalise this instantiation as version-controlled memory, in which synchronisation actions push and pull updates between private views, and mechanise it in Rocq. We show that Java programs that are correctly synchronised under the Java memory model behave identically under shared memory and Sync-as-Share.

title: DataHelix: A CPU-GPU Co-Scheduling Data Plane for Multimodal Model Training
summary: Multimodal model training breaks the loose coupling between data loading and model execution assumed by conventional training pipelines. Large per-sample variation in decoding cost, token/latent count, and tensor size causes both CPU preprocessing time and GPU compute time to vary substantially across data-parallel ranks (training processes). In synchronous training, these two sources of heterogeneity interact tightly: GPU execution determines how long the input pipeline has to prepare the next batch, while delayed preprocessing in any rank in turn stalls all GPUs at synchronization. As a result, optimizing CPU throughput or GPU load balance in isolation cannot eliminate pipeline bubbles. We present DataHelix, a metadata-first CPU-GPU co-scheduling data plane for multimodal training. DataHelix jointly reasons about preprocessing demand and GPU execution progress, treating each GPU compute window as the readiness budget for the next batch and coordinating preprocessing across ranks to minimize deadline misses rather than CPU makespan. To avoid expensive data movement, placement is decided while samples remain lightweight descriptors, before decoding and collation amplify them into large tensors. Descriptor-level token-latent-aware batching performs coarse pre-balancing, while cost-gated collective rebalancing corrects residual skew only when its expected benefit exceeds transfer cost. Across 11 video and multimodal workloads on 8 Ascend 910B accelerators, DataHelix reduces mean deadline-miss rate by 67.8% and mean p95 input-wait latency by 87.0%, while achieving 2.72x geometric-mean throughput over rank-local DataLoaders and 1.82x over a Ray actor pool under the same CPU budget.

title: MIRA: Mitigating Pole Geometry Bias in Recurrent Language Models
summary: We show that the Transformer's recurrent successors --- such as selective state-space models (SSMs), Receptance Weighted Key Value (RWKV), and Retentive Network (RetNet) --- can be characterized as infinite-impulse-response (IIR) systems. The zero--pole geometries of these IIR systems characterize the temporal modes they can represent. However, to trade parallelism, the algebraic structures of the parameterizations of these recurrent systems often give rise to poles constrained to the real axis, thereby inducing an architectural bias in their recurrent dynamics. To unify these recurrent architectures and eliminate their pole geometry bias, inspired by the lattice--ladder realization of general IIR systems, we present \textsc{Mira} (\textbf{M}odal \textbf{I}IR \textbf{R}ecurrent \textbf{A}rchitecture), a unified family of linear-time recurrent architectures for building large language models (LLMs) with a highly parallel algebraic structure. Each \textsc{Mira} block realizes a higher-order IIR system that represents temporal modes from token streams through a lattice--ladder structure, followed by a feed-forward network (FFN). This realization enables the model to represent the temporal modes associated with both real and complex-conjugate poles. We pretrain \textsc{Mira-S}, a 12-layer small-scale LLM with 0.14B parameters composed entirely of \textsc{Mira} blocks. Throughout the pretraining, \textsc{Mira-S} achieves lower perplexity than strong recurrent baselines, exhibits stronger context-window generalization beyond the training length, and attains higher throughput with a dedicated CUDA kernel.

title: Typed-Centrality Grounding for Agentic GraphRAG: A Symbolic Approach for Agentic Reasoning
comments: Preprint. 7 pages. Final version published in 2026 IEEE Symposium on Computers and Communications (ISCC), DOI: 10.1109/ISCC70364.2026.11739974
summary:
Knowledge Graphs (KGs) and Large Language Models (LLMs) represent two approaches for knowledge representation and reasoning over heterogeneous data. Recent research has explored their integration through Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) systems, which use KGs to provide structured context to LLMs. However, existing GraphRAG approaches treat KGs as homogeneous graphs and rely on textual similarity between the input prompt and the context, rather than using it as a source of deterministic knowledge.
  This work proposes an agent-based GraphRAG system that introduces a symbolic layer to integrate deterministic reasoning alongside text similarities. This approach is based on the definition of typed centralities for KGs, where centrality measures are computed separately for each specific KG's class. This information is used to construct a symbolic representation that is provided to the LLM as a deterministic source. The proposed system was mathematically validated and evaluated on a real-world POLE (Person, Object, Location, Event) dataset, comparing reasoning and information retrieval with and without the symbolic layer. The results indicate that the our approach leads to responses that are more consistent with the context, improving the generated outputs.
comment: Preprint. 7 pages. Final version published in 2026 IEEE Symposium on Computers and Communications (ISCC), DOI: 10.1109/ISCC70364.2026.11739974

title: Future-Informed Actor-Critic
summary: Actor-critic methods optimize a parametrized policy using a critic to estimate their policy gradient. Recent work has shown that conditioning the critic on features of future states, actions, or rewards can improve sample efficiency and even final return. However, existing methods are restricted to exogenous features (independent of actions), overlooking endogenous features (dependent on actions) that may be crucial for credit assignment. We introduce the future-informed value function, which can be conditioned on both exogenous and endogenous features of future states, actions, and rewards. Then, we express the policy gradient using this value function, yielding the future-informed policy gradient. Building on that, we propose the future-informed actor-critic algorithm. Empirical results show that this algorithm leveraging endogenous features of the future outperforms standard actor-critic algorithms in environments with noisy and sparse rewards.

title: DeepRadio: A Human-Agent Workspace for Physical Radio Development
summary: Agentic programming can automate software-defined radio (SDR) development, but decisions can propagate from software to hardware without sufficient user visibility or control. We present DeepRadio, a human-agent workspace embedded in GNU Radio Companion (GRC) for jointly constructing, verifying, and operating physical radio systems. DeepRadio uses a dynamic and state-driven workflow to coordinate a traceable radio specification, claim-oriented cross-layer verification, and mixed-initiative control. These mechanisms expose decisions, tie conclusions to available evidence, and return control to users before consequential hardware actions. Across seven atomic SDR tasks, DeepRadio completed nearly all runs while satisfying all prescribed software and radio-frequency constraints. In a 20-participant study, more participants achieved a verified physical deployment with DeepRadio than with Codex-assisted GRC. Participants reported stronger support for shared intent and understanding while retaining initiative and control. These results suggest that DeepRadio can make agent-assisted physical radio development more reliable, understandable, and controllable.

title: Improved Approximation and Hardness Bounds for $β$-TSP
summary: The traveling salesman problem (TSP) asks for a minimum-length Hamiltonian cycle in a complete weighted graph. Its approximability depends on the edge lengths: unrestricted instances admit no constant-factor approximation unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$, metric instances admit Christofides' $3/2$-approximation, and fixed-dimensional Euclidean instances admit a PTAS. We study $β$-TSP, where the edge lengths satisfy $ \ell_{uw}\leqβ(\ell_{uv}+\ell_{vw}) \qquad \forall\,u,v,w\in V\ \text{pairwise distinct}, \quad β\in\left[\tfrac{1}{2},1\right]. $ The condition arises naturally in various settings, for example, when metric travel times are combined with positive service times at the vertices. The previous best approximation algorithm, due to Böckenhauer et al., ranges from $1$ at $β=1/2$ to $3/2$ as $β$ approaches $1$. We obtain a strictly better guarantee for every $1/2<β<1$ by combining two simple constructions whose guarantees counterbalance each other. We also improve the best known approximation hardness bound for every $1/2<β<1$.

title: Robust & Scalable Website Fingerprinting via Minimal DRAM Traffic
summary: Website fingerprinting attacks infer websites visited by users and threaten their privacy. These attacks are classified as on-path, which monitor network traffic, and co-located, which exploit shared system resources. Existing co-located attacks, such as sweep-counting and loop-counting, achieve over 90% accuracy but suffer significant performance degradation on many-core systems. Loop-counting accuracy drops from 93% on 8 cores to 50% on 24 cores, while sweep-counting accuracy decreases from 84% to 45% across multiple Core Complex Dies (CCDs). To address these limitations, we propose memory-chasing, a scalable website fingerprinting attack that exploits DRAM traffic interference through pointer-chasing traversals with minimal interference. By counting DRAM accesses over fixed intervals, the attack generates distinctive traces for website classification. Evaluated on the top 50 websites, memory-chasing achieves 96% accuracy on a 24-core system, 86% across multiple CCDs, 80% across multiple sockets, and 97% in an open-world setting. Extensive evaluation across hardware configurations, browsers, operating systems, isolation mechanisms, system noise, and countermeasures demonstrates its robustness and scalability.

title: Agentic AI for Healthcare Claim Denial Analysis: A Policy-Grounded Framework for Privacy Preservation
summary: In the healthcare sector, claim denials impose significant financial and administrative burdens, emphasizing the need for automated and trustworthy decision-support systems. This paper proposes a modular Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) framework for healthcare claim denial analysis, integrating specialized agents for denial risk prediction, risk factor identification, diagnosis-procedure-medication code relationship analysis, and counterfactual analysis. The framework integrates predictive analytics, graph-based learning, a Hybrid Contextual Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline grounded in healthcare policy documents, and a dedicated HIPAA Compliance Agent to support privacy protection. Evaluated on a synthetic healthcare claims dataset, the framework achieved 98% traceability of reported numerical findings, validated 214 of 216 policy citations, and removed all 280 identified sensitive identifiers without modifying the underlying analysis. These findings pave the way for further research into Agentic AI as a framework for explainable, policy-aware, and privacy-preserving healthcare claim denial management.

title: MINE: Entropy-coded Memory-efficient Inference for Large Language Models
comments: Submitted to the 15th International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), 2027. Artifact: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23885927
summary: We present MINE (Memory-efficient INference Engine), a lossless entropy coding approach that accelerates single-stream inference of Large Language Models (LLMs), where existing lossless compression methods yield speedups only for specific data types such as BF16 and under additional assumptions. Single-stream decoding is strongly memory-bound, since every weight must be streamed from memory once per generated token and requests cannot be batched in local or low-latency deployments. At the core of MINE is dtANS-LLM, a GPU entropy coding scheme adapted from the prior dtANS to the needs of LLM inference. It exploits the non-uniform distribution of weights, which persists even after quantization, and exposes hyper-parameters that trade compression ratio against decoding cost. We auto-tune these parameters for each tensor and GPU to obtain the Pareto front between model size and decoding latency. MINE integrates into vLLM as a plugin and selects the best kernel configuration for a given memory budget. On Llama 3.1 8B Instruct with a 2.1-bit EntQuant checkpoint, MINE achieves speedups of 2.52x and 1.48x over the fastest baseline on an RTX 4060 Ti and an RTX 5090, at effective bitrates of 2.24 and 3.43 bits per weight. MINE is available as open source.
comment: Submitted to the 15th International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), 2027. Artifact: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23885927

title: EDP-PI-DOSnet: An Energy Dissipation Preserving Neural Solver for Two-Phase Flow Problems
summary: Preserving the energy dissipation properties of gradient flow equations is important for the stability and reliability of numerical approximations, particularly in long-time simulations. In this paper, we propose a class of energy-dissipation-preserving physics-informed deep operator splitting networks (EDP-PI-DOSnets) for solving gradient flow equations. The proposed framework incorporates classical structure-preserving numerical schemes into neural network architectures, allowing the corresponding discrete energy dissipation laws to be preserved. In particular, suitable constraints are imposed on the convolution kernels to ensure that the learned discrete operators are symmetric and negative semidefinite. Furthermore, several network formulations are developed based on the Crank--Nicolson (CN), scalar auxiliary variable Crank--Nicolson (SAV/CN), and relaxed discrete variational derivative (R-DVD-1) schemes. Meanwhile, a physics-informed loss function based on the residuals of the governing equations is employed. Numerical experiments show that the predicted solutions are in good agreement with the reference solutions while satisfying the corresponding discrete energy dissipation laws. The results also suggest stable behavior during long-time recursive prediction and the potential applicability of the proposed framework to two-phase flow problems.

title: DexDICE: Reconciling Safety and Performance via Dual-Expert Offline Imitation Learning
summary: Ensuring high returns while providing strong safety guarantees in offline imitation learning (IL) is a fundamental challenge: existing approaches either rely on explicitly specified cost functions, which are difficult to design for complex real-world safety constraints, or require expert demonstrations that are both safe and high-performing, which are often too costly to collect. We introduce dual-expert imitation learning, which leverages two complementary data sources: (i) safety-compliant demonstrations that faithfully follow safety guidelines but may be suboptimal, and (ii) performance-oriented demonstrations that achieve high returns but may violate safety guidelines. To address this problem, we propose DexDICE (Dual-expert offline imitation learning via stationary DIstribution Correction Estimation). Instead of conventional distribution constraints, DexDICE combines DICE-style offline learning with safe support constraints, enabling agents to exploit high-return behaviors while remaining within safety-compliant regions. We prove that the ideal solution satisfying this constraint exactly has zero unsafe-region visitation with high probability. We evaluate DexDICE on a re-curated DSRL benchmark and validate it on a real-world mobile-robot navigation task trained directly from human teleoperation demonstrations, where it substantially outperforms baselines and remains robust to data scarcity and quality degradation.

title: The Role Of Recurrent Refinement In Medical Image Segmentation
summary: While feed-forward segmentation networks perform well on large cohorts, they degrade in constrained clinical settings with few training samples and imaging artifacts. Human vision, by contrast, remains robust under these conditions, a property partly attributed to the recurrent and feedback connectivity of the visual cortex, which refines visual information over time. Inspired by this, we append lightweight recurrent refinement blocks to segmentation backbones, namely Conditional Random Fields (CRFs), modern Hopfield networks and convolutional GRUs, and study their behaviour as the number of iterations increases at test time (including beyond the training horizon). Evaluated on two open-source datasets, Kvasir- SEG and ARCADE, our recurrent blocks add less than 1.5% parameters and yield gains on clean data (up to 1.4 pp) and under noise (up to 17 pp) while reducing HD95. Code is available at https://github.com/joaodsmarques/recurrencehelpsegmentation .

title: Incentive Pathologies in a Live LLM Agent Arena: An Empirical Study of Concentration, Reward-Rule Implementation Discrepancy, and Network Dilution
comments: 29 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables; data available at Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23691548
summary: We audit one live LLM agent arena (AITRAP; 22 autonomous agent seats, ~96,000 reasoning nodes) over nine days (Oct 16-25, 2026), during which the platform deployed two bundled incentive changes: a progressive tax reform (V2.9.3, Oct 19) and a seed-inversion with explorer-side action update (V3.0, Oct 21). These serve as before-and-after markers, not cleanly isolated interventions. Four exploratory predictions are tested against ten data frames (F1-F10) using the Gini coefficient, Top-K concentration share, code-level reconstruction of the continuation-bonus mechanism, and the Mann-Kendall trend test. The Gini analysis is inconclusive at 95% confidence (bootstrap intervals straddle 0.7). The Top-4 node-activity-score share falls from 97.2% (Oct 19, pre-V2.9.3) to 49.4% (Oct 25, post-V3.0; 56.7% under a merge-seat assumption). The continuation bonus, announced as depth-based x10, resolves at code level to a four-condition anti-abuse gate paying x2.85 in the typical case and permanently blocking the self-continuation it superficially rewards; the gate was active ~40 hours before the V3.0 announcement. The events-per-node ratio declines significantly (Mann-Kendall S=-45, z=-3.94, p=8.3e-5) from 7.36 to 7.069. We discuss implications for incentive designers, the announcement-implementation gap, and public peer review as an event record.

title: Logit Laundering: Evading Data-Use Auditing in Large Language Models
summary: Data-use auditing in Large Language Models (LLMs) aims to determine whether the given data has been used for training, thereby supporting data ownership safeguards. A dominant solution is data watermarking, which embeds traceable signals into training data and detects them in model outputs. Recent studies have proposed many watermarking-based auditing methods in LLMs. However, systematic investigation from an adversarial perspective remains limited: non-compliant LLM providers would use unauthorized copyrighted datasets for training their own models to enhance model capabilities, while attempting to evade detection by auditors, thereby avoiding legal liability. To fill this research gap, we propose a novel evasion framework, termed Logit Laundering, where the non-compliant LLM provider manipulates model outputs at inference time to undermine detectable watermark signals. Specifically, we design a logit reshaping module to suppress watermark-induced statistical signals by integrating a statistical bias estimator as a plug-and-play component. This design keeps the model parameters unchanged and performs manipulation only in the logit space, thereby enabling auditing evasion while minimizing the impact on model's learned knowledge. To further balance evasion effectiveness and model utility, we introduce a confidence-aware scaling module to adaptively calibrate the suppression strength based on next-token prediction confidence. Extensive evaluations show that Logit Laundering can successfully evade existing various state-of-the-art auditing methods, significantly attenuating detectable signals, while preserving model utility on downstream tasks. Our work highlights the need for exploring more robust auditing methods to guard against evasion behaviors.

title: Additive $Ω(\log^* OPT)$ Gap for Bin Packing with Three Items per Bin
summary: We prove that bin packing is NP-hard to approximate within an additive factor of $o(\ls\OPT)$, even when all item sizes are arbitrarily close to $1/3$. This gives the first lower bound for bin packing with an additive factor that depends explicitly on the optimum value. In addition, we give a polynomial-time reduction from any bin packing instance into one with item sizes arbitrarily close to $1/3$, preserving its additive configuration-LP gap up to constant factors. Thus, in the sense of additive configuration LP gap and up to a constant, we confirm the conjecture that 3-partition instances are the hardest bin packing instances. In particular, we obtain an unconditional $Ω(\ls\OPT)$ gap for 3-partition instances. We build on the recent OpenAI construction that uses five items per bin and rules out any constant additive gap.

title: Not All Entropy Is Equal: Reward-Conditioned Entropy Allocation in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
summary: Policy entropy is widely used to diagnose exploration and collapse in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), yet its magnitude does not consistently track reasoning performance across optimization objectives. We argue that this ambiguity arises because global token entropy conflates uncertainty in successful and failed trajectories, diversity across correct solution strategies, and variation among realizations of the same strategy. We introduce \textbf{Reward-Conditioned Entropy Allocation (RCEA)}, a hierarchical diagnostic framework that separates complete-trajectory entropy from average token entropy, conditions uncertainty on verifier outcome and process validity, measures correct-solution-mode retention, and connects these population-level quantities to local covariance-driven updates. In controlled sweeps over six RLVR objectives at two model scales, entropy trajectories do not induce a stable ordering of reasoning accuracy. Token entropy is higher for verifier-failed than successful trajectories under both broad separately aggregated estimates and a common-question paired analysis, whose confidence intervals exclude equality at 10 of 12 displayed endpoints. A local covariance approximation predicts the direction of adjacent-checkpoint entropy change in 95.5\% of nonfailed transitions; a reward-stratified endpoint proxy further shows that positive chosen-token covariance is more tail-concentrated within failed prefixes. Every reportable trained endpoint exhibits some contraction in independently audited correct-solution-mode breadth, whose positive association with large-\(k\) coverage remains exploratory. These results show that entropy collapse should be diagnosed by which uncertainty is removed, rather than by global entropy alone.

title: From LoRA to Language: Recovering Skill Documents from Adapters
summary: Agent skills are short documents that teach a language model how to handle a class of tasks. To save context, these documents are increasingly compiled into low-rank adapters (LoRA), which keep the behaviour but lose the text: an adapter is hard to read, edit, audit or move to another model. We ask whether the skill document can be written back from the adapter and its frozen base model, and we score each recovered document by the share of the original's key instructions it states and by the tasks it solves. Reading the weights alone recovered little with the methods we tried; a learned map from weights to text passed on about one bit of the document. Running the adapter worked much better. The Executing Writer, a small writer trained on top of the adapted model, recovers 39-44% of the key instructions of held-out skills, against 1.3-1.5% with another skill's adapter, and on adapters fitted to 41 external skills its documents restore 85-91% of the original's task gain. These strongest results are on adapters whose training stored the document; adapters trained on behaviour alone are much harder for trained writers (1-2% of instructions). For these adapters we test an agent that runs the base and adapted models and writes a skill from where they differ. On ALFWorld its skills recover 58-71% of a LoRA's gain and carry over to models that cannot load the LoRA, lifting Llama-3.1-8B from 5% to 55%. Whether such a skill comes from the adapter depends on what the adapter learned: when its behaviour cannot be guessed, the adapter is the source; when it can, a reward loop without the adapter does as well.

title: Overview of the ImageCLEFmedical 2026 GANs task: Exploring fingerprint detection, privacy leakage, and synthetic medical image generation
comments: CLEF 2026 Working Notes, 21-24 September 2026, Jena, Germany
summary: The 2026 ImageCLEFmedical GANs Task Exploring Fingerprint Detection, Privacy Leakage, and Synthetic Medical Image Generation continues to investigate privacy and security concerns around using patient data to generate synthetic medical images, now in its fourth edition. This edition introduces three complementary subtasks: the first extends prior editions by asking participants to detect which real images were used in training a Generative Adversarial Network to produce given synthetic outputs; the second is a novel subtask requiring participants to identify which latent vector produced each synthetic image, probing the faithfulness and reversibility of the latent-to-image mapping; the third asks participants to generate privacy-preserving CT slices, quantifying the trade-off between image fidelity and patient privacy. Ground-truth annotations and benchmark datasets of real and GAN-generated lung CT slices are provided for all subtasks. Evaluation is based on Cohen's Kappa for Subtask 1, matching accuracy for Subtask 2, and a combination of FID and Privacy Preservation Score (PPS) for Subtask 3. Overall, 37 teams registered for the task, with 10 teams submitting runs across subtasks and 6 teams submitting working notes papers. This paper presents an overview of the task setup, datasets, evaluation metrics, and summarises the approaches and results of participating teams.
