Under group-relative optimization, however, a rubric that every sampled response fails (unreachable) or passes (saturated) gives all responses the same outcome and no learning signal; in Qwen3-4B medical training, 60.88% of query-rubric observations are inactive. We find that the two states lack different supervision: stating an unreachable rubric in the prompt raises its satisfaction from 1.13% to 91.25%, whereas responses that all pass a saturated rubric still differ in quality. We therefore propose RuACT (Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers), which assigns each inactive rubric the role that supplies what it lacks. Rubric as Teacher uses unreachable rubrics as privileged information for reward-gated on-policy self-distillation, and Rubric as Critic decomposes saturated rubrics into child rubrics that separate current responses while sharing the parent's weight. RuACT outperforms GRPO, rubric reweighting, and rubric-guided exploration on all four medical and scientific benchmarks with Qwen3-4B and achieves the best average with Qwen3-1.7B. On initially unreachable rubrics, unguided recovery rises from 35.02% to 42.86%, while child refinement improves reward-quality alignment on independent rollouts from 57.74% to 60.77%. Code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/RuACT.

title: Transformer-FSQ: Discrete Latents for Extreme KV-Cache Compression
summary: Private, personalised language models must run on local consumer devices, where large, frontier models cannot fit, and retaining long contexts is non-trivial. Sequential memory---the key-value (KV) cache---grows linearly with context length, quickly dwarfing the model itself: for Qwen3-1.7B-Base, 200,000 retained entries require 21 GiB, 6.6 times more than the model weights. Yet the KV-cache compression methods we measured fail beyond moderate compression ratios. We introduce Transformer-FSQ, addressing extreme KV-cache compression by replacing standard key and value projections with a finite scalar quantisation bottleneck. Our cache stores a packed vector of discrete integer codes per token, with no per-token quantisation metadata. Converting a pretrained transformer trains only these projections on 0.25 tokens per original parameter. We evaluate Transformer-FSQ against five baseline families on models from 0.6B to 8B parameters. On long-context retrieval (RULER), from 12$\times$ to 97.5$\times$ Transformer-FSQ is the most accurate method we evaluate, across scales. A fused Triton kernel decodes directly from the integer codes; with baselines given their authors' kernels where available, it decodes at $1.01\times$ (95% interval $0.98$--$1.05$) the throughput of native SDPA attention on the uncompressed Qwen3-8B-Base at $32\times$ and $1.54\times$ at $97.5\times$. Extreme KV-cache compression is therefore a practical way to extend how much context a fixed device can hold.

title: Dual-Region Slice Aggregation for CT-Based Renal Tumor Classification
summary: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) is the most common kidney cancer in adults. We present a region-aware architecture for CT-based ccRCC classification. Tumor and 0--10 mm peritumoral context are pooled separately from shared frozen DINOv3 feature maps. A shared position-aware slice aggregator precedes fixed training-only principal component analysis (PCA). The resulting representations are fused with radiomics using two scalar feature gates. Evaluation on KiTS23 and 111 external cases yields internal test and external AUCs of 0.8078\pm0.0154 and 0.9094\pm0.0015. Compared with matched single-tumor readout, mean AUC increases by 1.50 and 2.34 percentage points, respectively. Early-PCA and reconstruction controls yield lower internal mean AUCs, while external AUC is similar for early and late PCA. These findings highlight the joint role of regional readout and slice aggregation in adapting frozen visual features to renal CT.

title: Coresets for Capacitated Clustering via Dual Concentration
summary:
We study coresets for clustering problems, focusing on the classical $k$-median and $k$-means objectives. A coreset is a small weighted summary of the input data that approximately preserves the clustering cost for every choice of centers. Such summaries are a central tool for scaling clustering algorithms to large datasets.
  In this work, we consider the capacitated setting, where the clustering is subject not only to choosing centers but also to respecting prescribed cluster-size constraints. This model is a natural generalization of standard clustering and has been widely studied, but its coreset complexity is less well understood. For finite metric spaces, we obtain optimal-size coresets; surprisingly, these match the best-known bounds for unconstrained clustering. We also give improved coreset bounds in Euclidean space, notably the first coresets with near-linear dependence in $k$ while being independent of the dimension and input size.
  The main new technical ingredients are concentration bounds for the dual solutions of min-cost flow problems, which allow for both significantly simpler and tighter analyses of the underlying sampling distribution used in the coreset construction.

title: A Fast and Accurate Algorithm for the $p \to q$ Norm of Sparse Non-Negative Matrices
summary:
We present an algorithm that computes the $p \to q$ norm of a non-negative matrix with $s$ nonzero entries to accuracy $\varepsilon$ in time $\widetilde{O}(s^{3/2} \log (1/\varepsilon))$, for any $p \ge q \ge 1$. The fastest algorithm previously designed for this problem has running time $\widetilde{O}(s / \varepsilon)$ (Objois and Vladu, 2026), which is slower when high accuracy solutions are desired.
  Our algorithm employs a surprising application of Laplacian solvers inside an Interior Point Method (IPM). We formulate the problem as a linear optimization problem over a product of power cones, and show that the Newton updates of the IPM can be computed by solving a Laplacian system in a Schur complement after subtracting a rank-2 matrix.
  We also discuss an implementation of our algorithm, showing that it is practical and it outperforms optimized solvers such as MOSEK by factors of up to $20\times$ on a variety of tasks.

title: DKWBC: Decoupling Motion Tracking and Balancing for Humanoid Whole-Body Control
summary: Humanoid whole-body control requires a robot to track diverse reference motions while maintaining balance under gravity, torque limits, contact switching, and external disturbances. Existing reinforcement-learning-based trackers typically learn control outputs that jointly address motion tracking and balance. However, similar reference poses can correspond to substantially different dynamic demands, requiring a unified policy to learn motion-dependent control requirements alongside balance corrections. This can complicate learning and lead to high-frequency fluctuations in control outputs. We propose DKWBC, a dynamics-informed whole-body control framework that combines explicit model-based tracking with a learned balancing residual. Inspired by the model-based and environmental-wrench contributions to joint torques in floating-base dynamics, DKWBC uses inverse-dynamics feedforward and joint PD feedback to supply tracking torques, while a residual policy learns additional joint-torque corrections for balanced execution. By explicitly accounting for motion-dependent torque demands, this structure simplifies the policy's learning task. Experiments in simulation and on real hardware demonstrate that a single learned balancing policy generalizes across motion datasets while maintaining accurate motion tracking and balance across ground support, attached payloads, and physical interaction. Project page: https://robbyant-research.github.io/DKWBC/.

title: ReplayAudit: Auditing Outsourced LLM Fine-Tuning via Sealed Records and Selective Replay
summary: Auditing outsourced LLM fine-tuning requires checking an untrusted provider's training while controlling verification cost. Uniform sampling ignores training-time signals, while checking a suspicious record can require replaying several preceding steps. We present ReplayAudit, a telemetry-guided auditing system that seals training records before challenges and independently replays sampled intervals from sealed checkpoints. Loss changes and parameter-update norms guide stratified random sampling; replay determines whether the selected computation agrees with its records. We relate sampling probabilities to replay work and evaluate the system on real LoRA training. A 7B BF16 prototype rejects a false update-norm report during a random audit; targeted checks also reject false loss reports and skipped updates. We calibrate sampling budgets offline to at least a 90% probability of directly selecting an injected step. For two learning-rate deviation settings, executing these budgets on the same honest 1.5B trajectory reduces median complete-audit wall time by 49% and 67% relative to uniform sampling. When skipped updates evade the high-anomaly stratum, the corresponding audit instead costs 38% more. These results show how deviation capture and actual replay work jointly determine the cost of telemetry-guided auditing.

title: Not Your Diary, Just Your Topic: Grading the Wrong-User Control
comments: 21 pages. NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Personalized, Aligned, Long-Term Memory for AI Systems (PALM)
summary: A common test of personalization replaces a user's history with someone else's and measures the drop in accuracy. But this swap also changes the topics in the history, so the drop may reflect topic mismatch. We examine this problem with a frozen language model on LaMP-2 news categorization, using histories from similar users and synthetic histories assembled from other users' articles. The user's own history improves accuracy by 2.3 percentage points over a model trained without history. Removing history only at evaluation makes this gain appear larger, at 4.8 points. Category labels alone reproduce 86% of the accuracy gap between the user's own history and a random user's history. With synthetic histories matched on labels and text similarity, the gap falls to 0.9 points. Across two user splits and three training seeds, the advantage over a similar user's history is 3.2 points for users seen during training and 0.65 points for unseen users, where the evidence for an advantage remains inconclusive. A small movie-tagging experiment with one training seed also finds no advantage over other users' histories. These findings show why personalization should be evaluated on unseen users, with histories of similar content and a model trained without history as comparisons. We also find that adding gated cross-attention improves on a prefix-only model under our training setup; whether this holds more broadly remains open.
comment: 21 pages. NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Personalized, Aligned, Long-Term Memory for AI Systems (PALM)

title: Online Timely Bin Packing Revisited: A Simpler Algorithm with Optimality in Special Cases
summary:
Online Timely Bin Packing is a variant of classical online bin packing in which items arrive over time with sizes and deadlines. Packing an item may be deferred until its deadline, but once a collection of items is packed into a bin, the bin is closed and cannot be used again. The objective is to minimize the total number of bins used. The problem was introduced by Khattar in 2023. In 2025, Aminian proposed Discrete-Greedy, a deterministic online algorithm with a competitive ratio of exactly $2$, which remains the best-known upper bound. Its analysis is particularly simple; however, the algorithm requires maintaining a fractional simulation internally and may leave usable space in some bins unfilled.
  We propose Thrifty-Greedy, a simple deterministic online algorithm that does not require a fractional simulation. We prove that its competitive ratio is exactly $2$, matching the best-known upper bound. At the same time, the algorithm automatically achieves the optimal competitive ratio on two natural classes of inputs: it is $1$-competitive when all items have the same size, and $1.5$-competitive when every item has size in $\{1/3,2/3\}$. In contrast, Discrete-Greedy has a competitive ratio of at least $2$ on both classes.

title: Know What You Need: Efficient Activation Checkpointing
summary: Large Language Model training is increasingly constrained by memory capacity. Activation Checkpointing reduces activation memory by avoiding storing selected activations during the forward pass and rematerializing them during backpropagation, thereby trading memory savings for additional computation. Although this technique is essential for scaling model training, rematerialization can be prohibitively expensive, particularly for Transformer linear layers. Approximate computation could reduce this overhead, but conventional approaches either introduce errors that accumulate over the backward pass or fail to exploit information available from the initial forward pass. We introduce a novel approximate rematerialization method that can yield unbiased gradient estimates: using information collected during the initial forward pass, the method selectively recomputes only the most important layer components, either through greedy selection or randomized sketching. Ablation studies show that the resulting gradients closely match the exact gradients. When applied to feed-forward layers, attention layers, or both, our method can recompute only two-thirds of the layer components in a Llama-488M model, while increasing perplexity by just 1.7%, 1.2%, and 2.5%, respectively.

title: Contextual Search and Bilateral Trade with a Trace-Square-Root Potential
summary:
We present a unified potential method for contextual search and bilateral trade with one-bit feedback and obtain order-tight algorithms for both problems. Our framework starts from a Bayesian perspective in which the unknown target (for contextual search) and the unknown pair of valuations (for bilateral trade) are sampled from a known prior distribution. In that model, the decision maker bases its prediction on the posterior distribution, obtained by conditioning on feedback received in previous rounds.
  For Bayesian contextual search, we present an algorithm with a total loss bounded by $O(\mathrm{Tr} \sqrt Σ)$, where $Σ$ is the covariance matrix of the target's prior; and for contextual bilateral trade, our algorithm's regret is bounded by $O(\mathrm{Tr} \sqrt{Σ_S}+\mathrm{Tr} \sqrt{Σ_B})$, where $Σ_S$ and $Σ_B$ are the covariance matrices of the seller's and buyer's valuations.
  We then use ideas from this Bayesian setting and adapt a ``dual'' of this trace-square-root potential to the classical worst-case setting, where the target and valuations are chosen adversarially from the unit Euclidean ball. For both contextual search and bilateral trade, we obtain tight $O(\sqrt d)$-regret algorithms. These results match the existing lower bounds up to a constant factor and improve on the previous guarantees of $O(d\log d)$ for contextual search and of $O(d6^d)$ for bilateral trade.

title: SparseModesNet for coupled thermal-hydraulic-mechanical system in heterogeneous porous media
summary: Coupled thermo-hydro-mechanical (THM) models describe interactions among displacement, fluid pressure, and temperature in geothermal systems. Fine-mesh simulations over many time steps are costly, particularly with heterogeneous permeability and thermal conductivity or fracture networks that alter fluid and heat transport. Proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) reduces the number of unknowns but can require many modes because its reconstruction is linear. We apply SparseModesNet to reconstruct coupled THM solutions using a small set of selected modes and a neural-network nonlinear decoder. Starting from a larger collection of candidate modes, SparseModesNet selects modes to reduce reconstruction error rather than simply retaining those with the highest energy. We compare SparseModesNet with POD on three problems: a two-dimensional heterogeneous medium, a two-dimensional connected fracture network, and a three-dimensional geometry based on Utah FORGE fractures. We evaluate reconstructed displacement, pressure, and temperature fields, as well as pressure- and temperature-based quantities of interest. We also test temporal interpolation by training on a subset of snapshots and reconstructing omitted snapshots within the same time interval. For the same reduced dimension, SparseModesNet achieves smaller reconstruction errors than POD and accurately recovers the solution fields and selected geothermal quantities of interest.

title: CRTrack-Cap: A New Benchmark for Cross-View Dense Video Object Captioning
summary: Dense video object captioning (DVOC) localizes, tracks, and describes object trajectories within a video. Existing methods process each camera view independently, producing separate camera-local tracklets and captions for the same person across cameras. These outputs lack a unified description and leave complementary appearance evidence across views unused. We therefore formulate cross-view DVOC (CVDVOC), which associates these tracklets into scene-level global trajectories and generates one caption for each trajectory from synchronized views. To support this task, we construct CRTrack-Cap from CRTrack by auditing text-identity links and converting usable referring expressions into canonical captions. It retains 425 global trajectories and 838 local tracklets across 13 scenes, with canonical captions for 335 identities. We adapt CHOTA to the cross-view setting as CV-CHOTA to jointly evaluate tracking and caption quality. Our reference framework combines View-Exclusive Cross-Camera Association (VECA) for grouping tracklets with Conflict-Evidence Gating (CEG) for integrating caption evidence using its reliability and disagreement across views. Against three single-view methods adapted with MvMHAT for cross-view association, our framework achieves CV-CHOTA scores of 83.43 and 33.48 on the scene-disjoint in-domain and cross-domain tests, respectively. Together, CRTrack-Cap and our framework provide a benchmark and a strong baseline for describing the same person consistently across camera views.

title: BiLoGo: Reducing the smoothing of localised responses in Transformer-based neural operators for sheet forming
summary: Trial-and-error FE simulation of sheet forming could be computationally expensive, neural-network-based learned simulators are used to accelerate design. These simulators should accurately capture localised responses, such as thinning around sharp radii or near ribs, which determine formability. Transformer-based neural operators propagate information efficiently across the mesh but tend to smooth such localised responses. This study develops BiLoGo, a Bipartite Local-Global learned simulator with an FE-guided design that connects local node-element message passing with a Transformer-based neural operator for long-range information exchange. BiLoGo has three modules: a bidirectional node-element GraphSAGE model that learns nodal-elemental coupling on a bipartite graph and predicts each quantity on its native FE entity without interpolation; a dual-stream Transformer-based neural operator that processes blank deformation and tool contact with separate token sets, preventing localised contact information from being averaged with the whole-blank state; and a fusion and element update module that combines global and local features via gated residual fusion and updates element features conditioned on element-node kinematics. Evaluated on a dome-shaped cold forming case and two corner-shaped hot stamping cases (one with ribs), BiLoGo achieves the lowest positional and threshold-based thinning errors on all three cases compared with single-level and hierarchical graph-based models and Transformer-based neural operators. Near the ribs, the smoothing index of predicted thinning increases from 0.41-0.56 for Transformer-based neural operators to 0.94 for BiLoGo-U. Compared with the hierarchical graph network CAtt-BiUGNN, BiLoGo-T reduces mean positional error by 15.5% on the Corner case and BiLoGo-U by 8.3% on the Corner+Rib case, with 66-69% less training memory.

title: On Positive Computation
summary: We introduce new notions of reducibility for monotone classes and show that a monotone version of Circuit Satisfiability and the Hamiltonian Cycle Problem are complete for $mNP$, even under positive reductions (which are not the same as monotone reductions). If this holds for all (monotone) $mNP$-complete problems - that they are also so complete for $mNP$ -, then $P\neq NP$. We introduce positive models of relativized computation and show that the separation $posP\subsetneq mNP$ does not relativize, even when oracles are restricted to monotone sets. Yet, there is a (weak) diagonalization proof that $posP\subsetneq mNP$.

title: Entering a New Domain in the Era of Generative AI: An Autoethnography of Solo Game Development as a Bioinformatics Educator
summary: The rapid improvement of generative AI (GenAI) not only increased the efficiency of practice but also empowered individuals with capabilities to explore new domains. However, identity formation in the wake of such empowerment remains understudied. We use an autoethnography to understand identity formation in the context of solo game development as a bioinformatics educator. With the goal of developing a create-your-own-adventure (CYOA) game, we collected data for 73 days through journal entries, interacting with communities of practices. The autoethnographer had continuously reassessed the situation, and closely interacted with communities of practice. Their prior knowledge was used to provide in-game context and to uniquely interpret game development processes. These findings suggest that the autoethnographer made efforts to belong to communities of practice and engaged extensively in sensemaking through the lens of a bioinformatics educator. Although GenAI puts power at hand, attaining a new identity took place at a human pace.

title: TPIC: Energy-Conserving Space Plasma Simulations on GPU Supercomputers
summary: Artificial heating and numerical damping affect particle energization in kinetic space plasma simulations, even when the numerical scheme remains stable. Implicit and semi implicit energy conserving Particle-in-Cell (PIC) methods eliminate these errors in the discrete energy balance while relaxing explicit stability constraints. We present TPIC, a massively parallel implementation of the Energy Conserving Semi-Implicit Method (ECSIM) for GPU supercomputers. We extend the exact energy conservation in the ECSIM formulation to closed domains with conducting boundaries by deriving and canceling a spurious term in the discrete Poynting flux theorem. TPIC executes the complete particle and field cycle on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs, combining matrix-engine acceleration with asynchronous communication and computation. We validate TPIC in a variety of electrostatic and electrodynamic test cases relevant for space plasma physics applications, including quasineutral plasma expansion, two-stream instability, Whistler waves, Weibel instability, Whistler turbulence, and three-dimensional magnetic reconnection with conducting walls and 12.3 billion particles. We show that in all scenarios, TPIC agrees with the corresponding analytical theory or reference numerical results, and preserves the total system energy to machine precision. On 4,096 AMD GPUs, TPIC advances 1.9 trillion particles with 96.8\% weak scaling efficiency.

title: Encoding Memory in World Models with Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning
summary: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) approaches have demonstrated strong performance across diverse domains in recent years, learning accurate world models from agent trajectories. However, despite this progress, current approaches still struggle to surpass human performance on tasks that require long-term memory and planning. In this work, we address the problem of long-term memory in MBRL by moving beyond the commonly studied paradigm of architecture design. We introduce Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning (TT-MBRL), using gradient descent at test time to encode the memory of episode observations into world model parameters. This enables the agent to learn a distinct world model for each episode, improving memory capabilities compared to traditional approaches that solely rely on contextual memory. We first establish a proof of concept on a simplified two-dimensional variant of the Memory Maze environment, which we refer to as Memory Maze 2D, showing consistent improvements across different world model architectures. We then demonstrate the effectiveness of TT-MBRL in the 3D domain, achieving new state-of-the-art results on the Memory Maze benchmark. Finally, we show that TT-MBRL maintains strong performance on non-memory benchmarks such as DeepMind Control and Atari 100k.

title: A Novel Algorithm to Simulate Conductance-based Neuronal Networks
summary: Conductance-based models are central to neurophysiology and neuromorphic engineering, yet their simulation scales poorly to large networks. We study and analyze an iterative solver that operates in signal space. Each iteration reduces to $N$ decoupled scalar linear time-varying differential equations, one per neuron, which are solved in parallel and in closed form. The solver admits two complementary interpretations: a variable metric forward-backward splitting method, rooted in operator theory, and a waveform relaxation quasi-Newton method, rooted in circuit simulation. We prove uniform and superlinear convergence, with a bound that reflects the conductance structure of the dynamics. The algorithm is illustrated on the classical Hodgkin--Huxley neuron and on networks of up to 5000 neurons.

title: What remains of the planar induced minor conjectures?
summary:
Dallard, Milanič, and Štorgel, and independently Gartland and Lokshtanov, conjectured that for every planar graph $H$, Maximum Weight Independent Set and List $3$-Coloring are polynomial-time solvable in $H$-induced-minor-free graphs. As a structural explanation, Gartland and Lokshtanov further conjectured that such graphs admit balanced separators dominated by a constant number of vertices. Bonnet and Chang recently refuted the independent-set part of the algorithmic conjecture, by showing that Maximum Independent Set is $\mathsf{NP}$-hard in graphs excluding the $5\times5$ grid as an induced minor.
  We revisit both conjectures. We show that the graphs used by Bonnet and Chang exclude much simpler planar graphs, including several $16$-vertex trees, and we introduce a second, independent family of hard instances. We also prove that $3$-Coloring is $\mathsf{NP}$-hard in both settings, thus refuting the algorithmic conjecture in full, even in its quasipolynomial version, unless $\mathsf{NP}\subseteq\mathsf{QP}$. On the structural side, we identify planar graphs $H$ for which the structural conjecture holds, while the algorithmic one fails. Thus, constantly dominated balanced separators cannot by themselves explain the tractability of Maximum Weight Independent Set and List $3$-Coloring.

title: Steerable Multi-Objective Group-Relative Preference Optimization with Jointly Trained Low-Rank Adapters
summary: Language model deployment often requires different trade-offs between competing objectives as user preferences change, yet standard post-training methods typically produce a single policy for a fixed objective weighting. We introduce LambdaMix, a new parameter efficient method for learning a preference conditioned family of policies with group-relative online reinforcement learning. LambdaMix jointly trains one low-rank adapter per objective over a frozen base model. One preference vector selects the adapter mixture that generates responses and weights the separately normalized rewards used to update the adapters. A single training run supports changing preferences at inference without further optimization. We experiment with four models on helpfulness and harmlessness and on solving math problems while following instructions. We also evaluate the two largest models on rewriting comments to preserve wording while reducing clues about personal attributes. On the first two tasks, LambdaMix achieves higher hypervolume than all evaluated conditioned and policy merging baselines across all four models. LambdaMix uses fewer training completions and stores fewer adapter parameters than a set of GRPO specialist policies. With architecture and initialization fixed, varying adapter mixtures and objective weights together gives wider score ranges and higher coverage than varying either alone.

title: Capacity of Generic Symmetric Distributed Linear Computation: The Geometry of Relations
summary: In distributed linear computation, $K$ users observe linear functions of common finite-field data and send separate messages to a server that wants another linear function. We characterize the generic capacity $C$, the minimum total number of field symbols sent per computed instance, when all observations and the demand have dimension $ν$, the data have dimension $μ$, and the coefficients of these linear functions are drawn independently and uniformly from the field and stay fixed during coding, with the field size growing through arbitrary prime powers. For fixed $K$, $C/ν$ depends only on $τ=μ/ν$: the curve has finitely many linear pieces for at most three users, infinitely many pieces approaching one value of $τ$ for four users, and a rational part between two sequences of linear pieces for five or more users. The geometry of the relation space, formed by the linear relations among the observations and the demand, determines three things: the shape of the curve, which relations the coding scheme aligns, and the entropy inequalities used in the converse. Generically, the user subspaces of this space are either balanced, where the capacity lies on a single rational curve, or split into two balanced components, a sparse and a dense one, which produces the linear pieces. Achievability uses asymptotic set alignment, in which monomial precoders confine the combined observation differences to a small set. The converse uses the same geometry to lower-bound the sum of the users' remaining observation entropies in terms of the remaining data entropy.

title: LACART: Lookahead-Augmented Collision Avoidance and Reference Tracking Strategies for Safety-Critical Robots
summary: Autonomous racing provides a demanding testbed for collision avoidance under tight geometric and computational constraints. Building on a recent conference contribution and a master's dissertation, LACART combines lookahead-based control barrier functions (CBFs), a relaxed control Lyapunov function (CLF), and quadratic programming (QP) to modify nominal vehicle commands for obstacle avoidance and reference tracking. The method handles circular obstacles and track boundaries in a common optimisation layer. Comparative simulation results against Huang \emph{et al.} \cite{r9} show similar full-track paths and lower median computation times: 0.31 versus 0.33 ms per step and 0.023 versus 0.025 ms per QP solve. The dissertation further demonstrates a 1:43-scale vehicle with camera-based estimation and wireless actuation at a reported 25 Hz control rate. We identify the conditions linking lookahead-point clearance to body clearance, illustrate hardware limitations, and propose a recorded demonstration of safety intervention and recovery. The contribution targets ground-robot collision avoidance and real-time safety monitoring.

title: A Separation Principle for Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
summary: We study cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) problems in which agents evolve under decoupled noisy dynamics but share a population objective. A canonical example is a mobility operator that orchestrates a fleet of vehicles to meet customer demand. The stochastic and time-varying nature of these problems calls for learning approaches, yet existing MARL algorithms do not scale: learning assignment and routing jointly over the full state-action space becomes prohibitive as the number of agents grows. Formulating the problem over the space of probability measures, we prove a separation principle: the population cost-to-go function is upper bounded by an optimal transport problem whose transportation cost is the target-conditioned single-agent cost-to-go function. This simplifies the multi-agent problem to learning a single-agent policy and coordinating the agents via optimal transport. Building on this principle, we introduce SALT (Separation-based Assignment and Learning via optimal Transport), a family of algorithms that learn a target-conditioned single-agent policy using any standard reinforcement learning algorithm, and then coordinate the agents via optimal transport. Since learning occurs at the single-agent level, SALT scales to fleet sizes where MARL baselines become intractable and transfers without retraining to fleet sizes unseen during training. In a vehicle-delivery experiment on the southern Manhattan road network, where MARL baselines are computationally prohibitive, SALT improves travel time by 15-21% over a shortest-path routing heuristic. In stochastic grid worlds, SALT reduces average travel times by 23-61% relative to MARL baselines and scales to population sizes where these methods fail.

title: Fast and Actionable Classification of HPC I/O Time Series
summary: Input/output (I/O) is a major bottleneck for highperformance computing (HPC) performance. One of the challenges is the contention between jobs when sharing the parallel file system. However, tackling this issue depends on knowing the temporal behavior of jobs. In this paper, we propose a clusteringbased approach to characterize jobs' temporal I/O behavior. We propose SAGE, a lightweight method that cuts I/O traces into short windows and learns an alphabet from them. The trace then becomes a sequence of symbols, which we call ''genome'', and we use clustering to separate them into classes. We evaluate SAGE and its two-stage variant SAGE-2 on 819,771 real traces from 2 HPC systems. We compare them against other techniques from the state of the art on three metrics, including one we propose. Compared to K-shape, the best baseline available, SAGE-2 lowers the median intra-cluster metrics by 9.1% on average, and achieves this in 2 minutes of clustering time versus 3.8 hours, a 109x speedup. More importantly, clusters created by SAGE and SAGE-2 carry enough information to act on: we evaluate the use of the cluster centroids for I/O scheduling, and show that our approach can decrease I/O stretch by up to 24% compared to the state of the art (round-robin placement).

title: Parallel Algorithms for Higher-Order Temporal H-Index Computation
summary: Ranking vertices by importance is a fundamental task in network mining. The H-index provides such a ranking by asking how many neighbors are themselves well connected; its higher-order temporal variant recursively applies this idea over time-respecting neighborhoods in temporal networks. Scaling its computation is difficult because the existing streaming algorithm intertwines temporal processing with H-index order, incurring maximum-degree-dependent costs and exposing little parallelism. We show that the temporal dependencies can instead be resolved once: each edge's time-dependent lookup is mapped to a fixed successor position, turning every H-index order into a parallel gather followed by a segmented suffix-H computation. Based on this reformulation, we derive a linear-work suffix-H algorithm, a parallel multicore CPU implementation, degree-adaptive GPU kernels, and a multi-GPU scheme that exchanges only distinct remotely queried states. Experiments on synthetic and real-world temporal graphs show that the reformulation alone is substantially faster than the streaming algorithm, and that GPUs add order-round speedups exceeding an order of magnitude over our multicore implementation on synthetic inputs with up to one billion temporal edges. On a 636M-edge Reddit network, eight GPUs compute 128 orders in 3.6 s of round time, whereas the streaming algorithm does not finish within an hour even at order 8.

title: TensorMutation: Learning Weight-Space Mutations of Deep Learning Models on Neural Graphs
summary: Mutation testing for deep learning (DL) faces a cost-realism trade-off. The pre-training approach produces realistic but computationally expensive mutants, whereas existing post-training operators modify trained models efficiently but produce mutants that less closely resemble real faults. This study asks whether the trade-off is necessary: can the weight-space effect of a fault-informed pre-training mutation operator be predicted from a trained model, without retraining it? We answer this question with TensorMutation, which represents a trained model as a neural graph and uses a mutation-conditioned graph neural network (GNN) to predict parameter changes. The GNN is trained offline and reused across unseen models so that TensorMutation can generate executable mutants without retraining. We construct a corpus of 25,252 original-mutant pairs from 71 multilayer perceptron (MLP) classifiers using 11 fault-informed pre-training operators, including 25 newly curated subjects. TensorMutation partially reproduces the behavioral effects of pre-training mutations on nine held-out subjects, and direct weight-space supervision significantly improves weight-space fidelity. On 12 real-fault subjects, TensorMutation achieves the highest median behavioral similarity among the evaluated approaches. The improvement over the post-training tool DeepMutation++ is statistically significant (Holm-adjusted p=0.018), whereas the differences from the pre-training tool DeepCrime and the norm-matched random control are not significant. These results show that fault-informed pre-training mutations leave learnable structure in weight space that transfers to unseen models.

title: Concurrent Use of FP32 and FP64 Computing Units on GPUs and Mixed-Precision Placement in WENO Reconstruction
summary: Scientific computing often requires FP64 arithmetic, although FP64 performance is limited on NVIDIA GPUs. Double-float (DF) emulation, which represents a value using two FP32 values with about 48 bits of significand, outperforms native FP64 where FP64 units are limited. On the other hand, mixed-precision strategies offload to FP32 the operations that do not determine accuracy. In both approaches, the native FP64 units remain idle during FP32 instruction execution. We investigated whether this idle resource can be recovered on A100, GH200, GB200, and RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q. A microbenchmark shows that co-resident FP32 and native-FP64 kernels exceed the throughput of the faster kernel alone on A100 but not on GH200 and GB200; on RTX 6000 Blackwell, they do so against FFMA but, against DF emulation, only when the issue density of the DF kernel is reduced. We then tested whether this gain carries over to computing the WENO-Z reconstruction with the nonlinear weights in FP32 and the candidate polynomials in native FP64 (W32P64). We observe substantial overlap on A100, whereas GH200, GB200, and RTX 6000 Blackwell show little overlap. Importantly, the fastest placement does not always preserve the design accuracy of WENO-Z: for a one-dimensional entropy wave problem, W32P64 fails to achieve the design order of accuracy for WENO7 and WENO9. In contrast, DF emulation of the entire reconstruction comes close to it on the grids tested for WENO5, WENO7, and WENO9 while delivering a $2.51-3.94 \times$ speedup over FP64 on RTX 6000 Blackwell. For WENO5 on the two-dimensional Euler vortex problem the W32P64 error at $n=256$ is $1.26 \times$ that of FP64 and 1/104 of that of the all-FP32 reconstruction.

title: Breaking the Privacy Promise: Gradient Inversion Attacks on Federated Low-Rank Adapted Vision Transformers
summary: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) has been increasingly adopted to fine-tune pretrained models with low computational cost and is therefore also preferred in the federated learning paradigm to reduce computational and communication overhead. In this work, we investigate the sparsely explored problem of the risk of private data leakage in LoRA-adapted Vision Transformers (ViTs), where low-rank updates weaken the gradient signal available to a server with access to individual client updates. We show that quality of reconstruction is limited by two coupled ambiguities: reduced information in LoRA gradients and missing spatial cues from frozen positional embeddings. To address this, we propose a spatially anchored generative inversion framework that incorporates server-prescribed trainable positional embeddings into ViT blocks during fine-tuning at clients. The resulting positional gradients act as layer-wise spatial anchors, providing additional positional cues, while the generative prior keeps reconstructions on a realistic image manifold, reducing duplicate-data and patch-permutation artifacts, {which produce similar gradients as those produced when the target client images are used}. Adding our proposed spatial anchoring to GIAS improves PSNR by 10.14 dB, SSIM by 0.45, and LPIPS by 0.098 on CIFAR-10, as well as PSNR gains of 7.83 and 11.74 dB on high-resolution CelebA and CARS datasets, respectively, in the FedSGD setting. Such gains in reconstructed image quality metrics are also maintained at higher batch sizes and in FedAvg settings. These results indicate that LoRA-based PEFT does not, by itself, prevent data leakage in FL, and carefully incorporated positional embeddings can help in exposing private information.

title: Decoupled Mode Connectivity for Base-to-Novel Generalization in Vision-Language Models
comments: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 46 pages (10 main + references, appendix and checklist), 15 figures. Project page: https://iemprog.github.io/DMC/ Code:https://github.com/IemProg/DMC
summary:
Prompt learning adapts vision-language models such as CLIP by optimizing a short learnable prompt. The cross-entropy objective pulls this prompt toward
  base-class specialization, whereas generalization to unseen classes benefits from staying close to CLIP's zero-shot feature space. Because both objectives
  act on the same prompt, their gradients conflict at convergence, and in our experiments no single-prompt loss design clearly improves on the cosine
  baseline. We propose Decoupled Mode Connectivity (DMC), which gives each objective its own prompt. Starting from a base-trained prompt, DMC trains a
  specialization prompt and a generalization prompt, and merges their text features with a fixed coefficient at test time, at the inference cost of a single
  prompt. A linear mode connectivity (LMC) corridor in text-feature space keeps the classification loss low for every classifier interpolated between the two
  endpoints, and a Visual Anchor KL term preserves CLIP's zero-shot class-similarity distribution of each image during specialization. We further argue that
  such regularizers should satisfy class-permutation invariance (CPI), and show via Fano's inequality, in an idealized model, that violating CPI
  lower-bounds the drop in novel accuracy by a term proportional to the mutual information between the prompt and the base-class labels. Across 11 datasets,
  DMC improves the average harmonic mean of base and novel accuracy over MergeTune for both CoOp and KgCoOp, and its interpolation curves pass beyond the
  single-prompt operating point, shifting the base-novel frontier rather than trading along it. Code is available at https://github.com/IemProg/DMC.

title: From Function Inversion to Preimage Reporting
summary:
Given an arbitrary function $f:[N]\to[M]$, the function inversion problem asks to preprocess $f$ and to be able to, when given some $y\in [M]$, decide whether there exists some $x\in [N]$ such that $f(x)=y$ and if so, to report such an $x$. Recently, Fiat-Naor's solution to this problem has seen significant traction in theoretical computer science, and allowed for several conjectures related to meta-complexity and the 3SUM problem to be broken.
  In this paper, we consider the natural extension of the function inversion problem that we call preimage reporting. Here, instead of having to report only one $x\in [N]$ such that $f(x)=y$, the whole set $f^{-1}(y)$ must be found.
  We present a new general method to convert any arbitrary function inversion scheme into an efficient corresponding preimage reporting scheme. In particular, if $Δ$ is the maximal indegree of $f$, we show that we can perform preimage reporting using space $S$ in time $T$ for any $T$ and $S$ satisfying $TS^2=N^2 Δ$, matching a variant of a tradeoff obtained by Fiat and Naor for function inversion. This last result implies an improvement over the corresponding function inversion scheme itself, which constitutes the first function inversion scheme whose query time is inversely proportional to $|f^{-1}(y)|$. We derive new simple solutions for the $k$SUM-indexing with reporting and Jumbled indexing with reporting problems.

title: Differentially Private GraphRAG: Protecting Relation Connectivity and Semantics
summary: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) connects information across documents through entity relationships to support relational reasoning. However, black-box access to GraphRAG systems can enable adversaries to reconstruct knowledge graphs and recover both structural connectivity between entities and the semantics of their relationships. Existing defenses lack formal privacy guarantees and provide limited protection against such reconstruction attacks. We propose RelGuard, the first differentially private framework for GraphRAG, which provides formal privacy guarantees by mitigating connectivity leakage and protecting relations and their semantic meaning through relation removal. We formalize relation differential privacy (relation-DP), which bounds the distinguishability of mechanism outputs according to the semantic distance between alternative relations while accounting for relation removal. Building on this definition, we develop a four-step defense mechanism that sanitizes source documents before GraphRAG indexing by perturbing relation predicates or removing their associated connectivity using the exponential mechanism. Experiments across three GraphRAG systems and two targeted reconstruction attacks demonstrate that RelGuard provides stronger protection against reconstruction attacks than four existing defense mechanisms while better preserving downstream utility.

title: Video2Asset: Online Construction of Persistent 3D Street-Scene Assets
summary: Online 3D street-scene asset construction turns multi-view video into a continually updated scene of independently editable objects. The central challenge is to accumulate partial, intermittent observations under motion and occlusion without fragmenting identities or mixing evidence across objects. To address this challenge, we propose Video2Asset, an online framework for constructing persistent 3D assets from multi-view video. Using occupancy as an intermediate representation, we construct identity-aware observations with Historical Carrier Guidance for instance decoding and an identity encoder fusing instance-aligned 3D features with multi-view appearance. Accumulated-Evidence Association compares current observations with identity, geometric, and appearance evidence accumulated within asset records to determine identity inheritance and update world-coordinate states. We instantiate meshes from an asset library using these states and combine them with an occupancy-derived static background to support scene visualization, mesh replacement, object deletion, and trajectory editing. Experiments on several datasets demonstrate improvements in temporal identity consistency and asset quality across multiple occupancy models, including a 15.4% reduction in asset fragmentation on nuScenes with SGE.

title: How Much Conversation History Does an AI Agent Need?
summary: How does using less conversational history change reader-token use and benchmark scores? We examine this question on 1,100 BEAM questions. We held the retrieval ranking and reader constant across five fixed passage budgets, and mean assigned scores rose as the passage budget grew. The score gain per additional token became smaller at the upper tested budgets. Answerable questions generally received higher scores with more context. Pooled abstention scores sometimes rose as the passage budget shrank. We also tested message retention in a controlled task with explicit conversational-state targets and compared retained user messages with token-matched recency. Qwen matched the full state more often for direct requirements when user messages were retained. Its full-state matching declined when answers depended on references to earlier offers. Mistral produced near-floor results across the retention conditions. A scoring audit leaves the correctness of BEAM answers unresolved. These experiments characterize the token and score consequences of the tested memory budgets. Reliable budget selection depends on retaining the evidence each question requires and validating the measure used to assess answer quality.

title: Dual Architecture Fusion Vehicle Lidar 3D Target Detection
summary: In this paper, a 3D backbone network (SpconvTransformer) based on the fusion of convolutional architecture branch and Transformer architecture branch is proposed. The convolution branch uses 3D sparse convolution and submanifold convolution to learn local voxel features and semantic information, and the Transformer branch uses the self-attention mechanism to model the remote relationship between voxels, uses the broad receptive field to capture rich context information, and complementing the advantages of the two architectures by fusing the local features extracted from the two branches and the global features solves the problem of limited receptive fields of 3D convolutional neural networks. The experimental results show that the average accuracy of SpconvTransformer in 3D object detection and bird's-eye view detection tasks reaches 81.45% and 88.09%, respectively, and the average directional similarity reaches 91.10%, which is significantly better than other existing algorithms.

title: Online Causal Configuration for Networked Systems via Doubly Robust Steady-State Learning
summary: Measurement exploration reveals how interacting local controllers behave but can alter the steady-state regime a network operator seeks to optimize. Exploratory rewards may therefore fail to identify a configuration's no-exploration value: under full exploration, identical logged distributions can conceal different target values. Identification requires accounting for both action-law mismatch and shifts in the steady-state context distribution. We introduce CAUSAL-UCB, which selects configurations using optimistic bounds on target causal values. Its interference-aware clipped doubly robust evaluator produces predecision certificates separating statistical variation from calibrated identification, transport, and temporal-dependence errors. For any finite horizon and predetermined schedule of measurement-exploration rates $\{η_t\}$, we prove lower bounds of $Ω((1+\sum_tη_t)^{-1/2})$ on minimax inference error and $Ω(\sum_tη_t)$ on measurement-induced deployment loss in a stationary, potentially slow-mixing family. We bound regret under valid certificates and selected-information growth, and establish an anytime finite-sample certificate with a shared radius for estimation, selection, and reporting in a restricted known-local-interference model. In a high-mismatch benchmark with 24 paired seeds and 200 rounds, CAUSAL-UCB attains target regret of $1.732$ versus $6.326$ for certified IPS-UCB, with deployment gaps of $30.607$ and $23.217$, respectively. Independent-audit coverage tests and trace-driven semi-synthetic studies further assess certificate coverage and deployment trade-offs.

title: Goodhart in the Planner: Sampling-Based Control Exploits Rewards Learned from Human Preferences
comments: 19 pages, 4 figures. Equal contribution. Code and results will be released
summary: Robots increasingly choose actions by searching against a reward model learned from human preferences, in model-predictive control or best-of-$N$ selection; we measure what this does to the true objective. On HalfCheetah and Hopper with crowd-sourced labels, and on Meta-World drawer-open and plate-slide with synthetic labels and blind labels from the two authors, harder MPPI search cuts true return by up to 76%: with human labels the drawer opens in 0 of 20 runs against 10 of 10 for the cloned policy the planner starts from, while held-out label accuracy stays at 0.75-0.97. On plate-slide human labels are exploited less than synthetic ones, and on window-open search helps. True return roughly follows how far the planner's weights move from its proposals ($\sqrt{\mathrm{KL}}$) for both weighting rules we test, and best-of-$N$ with a verifier from synthetic labels falls below a single noisy action. We prove that $χ^2$-regularized MPPI at a temperature set by the scorer's error spread on the proposals is worst-case optimal, that no positive gain can be certified once that spread exceeds the scorer's own, and that an episode's return splits exactly into per-step terms, of which the guarantee covers the selection terms. Calibrated from 100 proposal pairs ranked by true return (an oracle) on start states the evaluation never uses, this rule is the safest fix we test: with each of five independent sets it succeeds in every arm run and keeps on average 86-94% of the cloned policy's return on plate-slide and drawer-open, though it is cautious where search helps. Calibration from a person's comparisons cannot detect a bias the scorer learned from that person; correcting for the pairs people cannot tell apart, or a second person, limits the damage.

title: ODEAction: From Predicting Chunks to Evolving Actions
comments: 23 pages, 5 figures, including appendix. Technical report
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models typically generate actions in chunks, organizing continuous robot execution into separately predicted segments and thus introducing potential discontinuities at action-chunk transitions. We propose ODEAction, a chunk-free action generation paradigm that replaces action-chunk prediction with Continuous Action Evolution. Given visual observations, language instructions, and robot proprioceptive information, ODEAction learns an action transition field defined over action space, where a transition vector characterizes the evolution rate of the current action with respect to evolution time. During execution, the model takes the current action as its initial condition and integrates the learned field using an ordinary differential equation (ODE), recursively generating subsequent actions with explicit dependencies. ODEAction is implemented as an action head and does not depend on a specific vision-language backbone architecture. Experiments on LIBERO, EBench, RoboTwin, and real robots show that ODEAction improves both task performance and trajectory quality over matched action-chunking baselines, with particularly pronounced gains on fine manipulation tasks.
comment: 23 pages, 5 figures, including appendix. Technical report

title: Nonlinear Fault Tolerant Control of Wind Turbine Pitch Systems: A Comparative Study
summary: Electro-hydraulic pitch systems account for about one fifth of wind-turbine failures, motivating the development of resilient control strategies for fault mitigation. The study considers a large set of robust nonlinear control designs of different feedback principles and architectures, and assesses their fault-tolerant capabilities in comparison to each other and against the industrial standard, i.e. the Proportional-Integral (PI) controller. The implementation and tuning of each scheme is based on a high-fidelity simulator to ensure nominal performance, whereas each controller is deployed unchanged on an experimental apparatus that includes a full-scale electro-hydraulic pitch system. The comparative evaluation of the considered fault-tolerant solutions is carried out through several tests that cover nominal operation and twenty-five representative fault scenarios, including sensor, process, and actuator faults. The analysis highlights the trade-off between performance preservation under faults and increased actuator chattering. The experimental results show that introducing a dynamic input-reconstruction module into the design of the nonlinear controllers significantly reduces actuator chatter without compromising their fault-tolerant properties.

title: Calibrating demand models versus adjusting OD matrices with traffic counts: a controlled comparison
summary: Traffic counts are routinely used to calibrate travel demand models, particularly when the origin-destination (OD) matrix is not observed directly. An important modelling decision is whether to adjust individual OD flows or the parameters of the demand model that generates them. The latter approach uses fewer parameters and preserves a relationship between zonal characteristics and demand, but its accuracy depends on the assumed model structure. We compare three established approaches using the same prior information, traffic counts and equilibrium assignment. They estimate five production-gravity coefficients, origin and destination adjustment factors, or individual OD flows. Synthetic experiments on the Eastern Massachusetts and Chicago Sketch networks allow recovery to be assessed against known demand under different forms of model misspecification. Calibrating the five-coefficient model gives better OD recovery and held-out link-flow prediction when demand follows its assumptions or a two-purpose gravity process. Its advantage declines or reverses when destination choice or production relationships vary across zones. Cellwise adjustment achieves the closest fit to calibration counts in 65 of 66 evaluated conditions, yet it recovers OD demand least accurately of the three approaches in 45 of them. These findings show that model parameterisation matters beyond calibration fit. For transport planning, traffic counts should be used alongside independent evidence on trip production and distribution when selecting and validating a demand model.

title: Autonomous Particle Image Velocimetry Using Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Reinforcement Learning
summary: Particle image velocimetry (PIV) reconstructs a flow field from the motion of tracer particles but the reconstruction quality is bounded by how well the flow structure of interest is resolved in the images. The acquisition position is typically fixed by the operator before the measurement. We cast camera placement as a sequential decision-making problem and train a reinforcement learning agent to control a 6-DoF manipulator equipped with a camera, enabling it to locate, frame and resolve a hydrofoil wake in a water tunnel. The agent commands the camera pose and observes the scene only through the velocity field and uncertainty estimated from time-separated image pairs. It is trained entirely in a photorealistic simulation of our water tunnel, with wakes generated by Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations of hydrofoils with varying profiles, positions and angles of attack. After zero-shot transfer to the real water tunnel, the policy reliably locates and frames the wakes of randomly placed hydrofoils. It resolves the wake at a higher resolution than a fixed camera view and with lower error in the measured flow statistics, in roughly half the time of a full scan and with far fewer image pairs.

title: SPARSEUP: Towards Better Recipes for Training Modern Learned Sparse Retrievers
summary: Learned sparse embeddings are a powerful alternative to dense retrieval, yet they have fallen behind single-vector and late interaction models. One reason for their limited adoption is that they are notoriously difficult to train, generally requiring very tight conditions to converge. We present a recipe for training Splade-like encoders on modern backbones and data that achieves a better efficiency-effectiveness trade-off. We discuss the role of logit distribution and its impact on the training stability and the final sparsity of the encoder. We also introduce a new per-position fan-out control - a hard cap on how many vocabulary dimensions each position may emit. We further apply a simple vocabulary merging strategy that removes redundant entries - such as case and word-boundary variants of the same word - which are common in cased BPE-based backbones. We apply our recipe to the LateOn backbone and training data, obtaining SPARSEUP, a sparse encoder that reaches 56.4 average nDCG@10 on BEIR-13, the highest we know of among public vocabulary-based sparse encoders below 150M parameters.

title: The Multiscale Single-Index Model: An MSE Analysis of Online SGD Dynamics
summary: We consider the Multiscale Single-Index Model (MSIM), first introduced by Oymak and Soltanolkotabi (2021), as a stylized model for hierarchical feature learning with scale separation. Each layer extracts a shared single-index feature at one physical scale and passes it to the next, giving a tractable setting in which to study how deep architectures learn local multiscale representations. Under non-degeneracy and delocalization assumptions on the link function and planted features respectively, for the two hidden-layer case ($K=2$), we analyze joint online spherical SGD under MSE loss, which is a canonical regression objective, in discrete time and show that it achieves weak recovery from random initialization in $O(d\log^2 d)$ samples, followed by strong recovery to accuracy $\varepsilon$ in $O(d\log(1/\varepsilon))$ additional samples. The main technical challenge arises from the non-Gaussian learned features observed by the second layer. We address this challenge through a quantitative Gaussian comparison using delocalization, combined with sharp trajectory-level control of the coupled SGD dynamics. This work is a companion to Bruna (2026, arXiv:2607.03347), which studies recovery under a correlation objective for general $K$.

title: SURE:Spatiotemporal Uncertainty Representation for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Learning
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies have become a promising paradigm for end-to-end robot control, but their effectiveness still depends heavily on large volumes of demonstration data. In manipulation tasks, this dependence is compounded by structured spatiotemporal uncertainty in the action space: multiple nearby actions or trajectories may successfully solve the same task, while semantically equivalent demonstrations often unfold at different speeds. Standard pointwise supervision treats each demonstrated action as an exact target, imposing an unnecessary learning burden under such uncertainty. We present SURE, a data-efficient VLA training framework that explicitly models both spatial and temporal uncertainty. SURE augments a VLA backbone with a lightweight transposed-convolutional probabilistic action decoder that captures spatial uncertainty through local correlations among neighboring action bins. It further introduces Soft-DTW alignment supervision to accommodate local timing variations between predicted and demonstrated action chunks. Together, these two components reduce sensitivity to demonstrator-specific poses and execution timing, enabling more data-efficient action learning. We evaluate SURE on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world manipulation tasks. Even with only 10% of the demonstration data or 20% of the training steps, SURE achieves manipulation success rates that match or surpass baseline VLAs.

title: PoseRieFlow: Riemannian Flow Matching for Whole-Body Text-to-Pose Generation
summary: We present PoseRieFlow, a compact flow-matching framework for text-conditioned generation of whole-body 3D human poses. Prior text-to-pose methods either neglect articulated hands or model rotations in Euclidean space despite their non-Euclidean geometry. PoseRieFlow instead formulates generation directly on the product manifold of SMPL-H joint rotations, learning a text-conditioned vector field that transports samples from an isotropic $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ Gaussian prior to the data distribution along Riemannian geodesics. A part-tokenized Diffusion Transformer aggregates the 52 joints into eight body-part tokens, allocating a dedicated token and nonlinear projector to each hand, and restores per-joint resolution through part-specific decoders, shortening the sequence while improving kinematic fidelity over per-joint tokenization. With only 21.6M trainable parameters, PoseRieFlow supports expressive SMPL-H generation with detailed hand articulation at a fraction of the scale of recent LLM-based generators. On PoseScript, it attains the lowest whole-body kinematic error among all hand-producing methods, with consistent kinematic gains from the Riemannian formulation over its Euclidean counterpart at every practical inference budget, while distributional and retrieval metrics remain comparable between them.

title: Real-Time Self-Penetration Repair for Skinned Characters with Soft Contact Budgets
summary: Motion that is plausible on one body can penetrate another after a change in shape, and motion models can produce self-penetration on their native characters. We present a training-free post-process that reduces these artifacts through pose correction followed by bounded skin compression. The module attaches to any motion model whose native character and output character have compatible character packs, without access to model internals. Each pack is built offline from the rig and skin without training. A vertex-level pose layer solves a local quadratic program in plain C on one CPU core, and a stateless contact deformer acts on the host's final skinned mesh. A part-dependent soft-tissue budget allocates correction between pose and skin through a static convention. Source penetration contributes no extra allowance; optional cloth thickness and compliance modify the pose layer's collision surface. Operation is causal or uses a short buffered lookahead, with frame-exact pass-through at the native interface for clean, inactive frames in the zero state. Across 320 unseen clips and 3 body shapes, the fraction of frames with hand-torso depth above 20 mm falls from 15.53% for copied motion to 0.00%, with final maximum depth 9.3 mm over every frame. Mean pose and skin costs are 1.11 and 1.18 ms, respectively, and their sum of 2.29 ms is a sub-frame processing cost. The median joint-velocity high-frequency ratio relative to copied target motion is 1.008.

title: Verifier Noise Is a Temperature: Testing Tilt Predictions in Finite-Budget LLM-Guided Search
comments: 34 pages, 5 figures. Pre-registered predictions, code and data checksums are described in Appendix C
summary: LLM-guided search loops propose a modified candidate, score it, and keep it if it scores better. When both candidates are re-scored at every comparison, as in the minibatch acceptance gates of prompt optimizers, keep-if-better is a reversible Markov chain if the score difference is logistic and the mutation operator is reversible, and its stationary law is the mutation equilibrium tilted by exp(beta f). For any continuous symmetric noise difference the same tilt is the stationary law of a small-step diffusion limit, with beta = 4F'(0); for a minibatch gate beta grows with the square root of the minibatch size. Caching the incumbent's score instead inflates the recorded score. We test the tilt as a prediction for LLM-guided program search, committing each prediction from calibration data before the search runs. The level after 150 steps rises with the minibatch size in six of seven settings, but its predicted value fails: on bin packing, search attains 62-88% of the predicted gain when the proposer edits the parent and 109-119% when it writes new heuristics. The attained fraction falls with the parent-child quality correlation of unselected mutation; a registered test on two new settings confirmed the direction, but not the quantitative agreement after a correction. Further registered tests found that runs started from a good program kept losing quality over 300 steps, more so from starts that search had selected, by a margin that passed its registered rule narrowly. Runs from different starts had not reached a common level, so whether the tilt describes the stationary law of LLM editing remains open. A registered test in prompt optimisation on frozen task-model scores failed: search exceeded the tilt, and the bin-packing relation did not transfer.
comment: 34 pages, 5 figures. Pre-registered predictions, code and data checksums are described in Appendix C

title: Attend at the Right Resolution: Head-Adaptive Sparse Attention via Query-Key Interaction Structure
summary: Attention is a major scalability bottleneck in large language models (LLMs), with its computational cost and key-value (KV) memory traffic becoming increasingly prohibitive as context length grows. Sparse attention addresses this bottleneck by restricting each query to a subset of the context, but its effectiveness hinges on identifying relevant regions both cheaply and reliably. Existing training-free methods primarily rely on runtime relevance estimates, with selection dimensionality and granularity typically governed by fixed heuristics rather than the intrinsic interaction structure of pretrained attention heads. We take a different perspective: the query-key operator of each pretrained head defines a characteristic response structure that determines the resolution needed for sparse selection, both across feature directions and across context tokens. Building on this insight, we propose Head-Adaptive Sparse Attention (HASA), a training-free sparse attention framework that jointly adapts selection resolution along these two dimensions. Along the feature dimension, the singular spectrum of each head's query-key operator determines an effective rank, yielding a compact, head-specific response space. Along the sequence dimension, neighboring regions are progressively merged according to the directional coherence of their token responses in this same space, while heterogeneous regions remain separate. Exact attention is then computed using the original full-dimensional KV states of the selected regions. HASA captures 88.1% of dense-attention mass and, compared with UNIQUE, a strong recent sparse-attention baseline, improves accuracy by up to 3.47 and 2.57 points on RULER and LongBench-Pro, respectively, and accelerates self-attention by up to 1.32x, while achieving up to 14.07x speedup over dense attention.

title: Adaptive PD-like Fault Tolerant Controller for a Class of Nonlinear Systems
summary: The article presents a nonlinear adaptive control strategy for a class of feedback-linearizable systems subject to process faults and disturbance. The controller is derived through Lyapunov analysis and incorporates an adaptive proportional gain within a PD-like structure, preserving simplicity while providing nonlinear adaptive behavior. A residual-based gating mechanism activates the adaptation only when the tracking error exceeds a prescribed threshold, preventing unnecessary gain updates during nominal operation and improving robustness to noise. The proposed design yields uniform global ultimate boundedness of the closed-loop signals, with explicit expressions for the steady-state tracking bound. Practical tuning guidelines for the adaptive parameters and Lyapunov matrix selection are provided to ensure consistent gating behavior. Simulations on a precision positioning system illustrate effective compensation of process faults, rapid gain escalation during degraded conditions, and smooth reversion to nominal performance, demonstrating that the method enhances fault tolerance while retaining the structural simplicity of PD control.

title: Empirical Study of Post-Quantum Cryptography Adoption Status in SSH Infrastructure
summary: With the anticipated arrival of Q-day, quantum computers threaten current cryptographic schemes for encryption and digital signatures. In response, major content delivery networks and cloud service providers are already adopting Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC). The current state-of-the-art focuses on benchmarking the operational performance of implementing PQC, but the real-world adoption status remains under-researched. This work utilizes large-scale SSH fingerprint data from a proprietary scanning tool to analyze PQC adoption across 1.52 million hosts and 27,012 entities. Our study shows that the PQC transition in the SSH protocol is underway but highly polarized: 45.2% of SSH hosts on port 22 support PQC, while 54.8% remain classical-only. At the entity level, 39.9% have enabled PQC on at least one host, whereas 60.1% have no PQC support. By correlating PQC adoption with industry, geography, and organizational size (digital and financial), this study provides a comprehensive empirical assessment of PQC adoption status in SSH infrastructure.

title: Finite-time Cholesky Factorization
summary: We propose an algorithm for estimating the Cholesky factorization of positive, semi-definite matrices without pivoting. Our method has the same data access pattern as the canonical Cholesky method, and therefore is amenable to familiar hardware optimization techniques. Our method interprets the factorization task as a variational problem and in turn solves it using an induced dynamical system. We study the rate of convergence of this dynamical system to its stationary state for both positive definite and semi-definite matrices. Numerical experiments validate that our method is competitive with pivoted Cholesky on several practical examples.

title: Empirical Assessment of Post-Quantum Cryptography Adoption Status in TLS
summary: Anticipating Q-day security concerns, major CDNs and cloud providers are migrating to post-quantum cryptography (PQC). While existing literature benchmarks PQC performance, empirical research evaluating real-world adoption data remains scarce. We present an empirical assessment of PQC deployment across seven critical protocols (HTTPS, LDAPS, SMTPS, IMAP-SSL, POP3-SSL, TELNETS, and RDP) using 10,000 target IP addresses per protocol. At the origin-server level, PQC algorithm support reaches 9.1% for HTTPS and 7.39% for LDAPS, while falling below 1% for all other evaluated protocols. At the entity level, PQC support is 11% for HTTPS and 5.4% for LDAPS, while the remaining protocols have less than 5% of entities supporting PQC on the hosted servers. We further correlate these adoption trends against organizational digital and financial footprint, and industry sectors, yielding a multi-dimensional empirical assessment of PQC deployment. Finally, at the domain level, we perform a comparative analysis of PQC adoption in Cloudflare-hosted domains against baseline Cloudflare datasets. Collectively, our findings provide critical insights into the current state of PQC readiness over Transport Layer Security (TLS).

title: A wearable input/output interface learns personalized models of haptic perception
summary: Wearable haptic interfaces deliver physical stimuli to the skin, yet perceived locations vary widely across users and diverge from actuator locations, particularly for emergent tactile-feedback techniques. We developed a wearable haptic input/output (I/O) device integrating a 36-channel electrotactile array with capacitive touch sensing, enabling stimulation and user-reported percept locations to be registered within the same body-referenced coordinate frame. In 24 participants, the device revealed electrotactile and referred-thermal perceptual maps with notable interparticipant variability. Despite this variability, both modalities retained electrode-pair-specific spatial structure across participants. Tactile and thermal percepts also showed spatial correspondence, whose strength varied across participants. These findings motivated our human-in-the-loop calibration framework, which adapts a forward-prediction strategy to individual users and generates personalized perceptual models. These models enabled inverse rendering by selecting stimulation patterns predicted to generate a target percept for a specific user. Using these models, we demonstrate personalized haptic rendering in haptic-guided robot teleoperation, visual-to-haptic sensory substitution, interpersonal haptic communication, and virtual reality (VR). Together, this platform provides a route toward adaptive haptic interfaces that measure, model, and render according to each user's perception.

title: RidgeFill: Training-Free Late-Layer Cache Fill for Faster Prefill
comments: 50 pages, 15 figures, 38 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/Approximate-Science/ridgefill-data
summary:
RidgeFill shortens prefill by not computing most of a model's upper layers for the prompt. The lower layers run exactly up to a split; from the split layer's state a per-layer map predicts every later layer's input, and each late layer writes its cache from that prediction. The design follows YOCO and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, where the projection is trained into the model. RidgeFill retrofits it onto models that were never trained for it: the map is a ridge regression fitted once in closed form from one pass over calibration text, the layer's own projections run unchanged, and a chosen set of rows, the last few thousand tokens, and every decoding step run the full model. Nothing is trained and no token is dropped.
  Most of the work was in measurement, finding a repeatable methodology. Loss averaged over all tokens hides RidgeFill's error. Needle retrieval in the filled region, loss on tokens that depend on distant context, and splice tests that swap filled keys or values for exact ones show which component carries it: the keys on Llama-3.1-8B, half of it in their scale, and the values and the recurrent state on Qwen3.5-9B.
  On Qwen3.8-27B in a llama.cpp fork on an A100, time to first token is 1.25 to 1.31x faster at 16K to 120K tokens with the maps in VRAM; RULER changes by -1.2 and -1.4 points and LongBench v2 by -1.4; the 95 % intervals include zero but do not rule out losses of a few points. On Qwen3.8-Flash-Next in vLLM it is 1.50 to 1.60x faster than exact at 9K to 32K tokens, with RULER's needle tasks at 99.8 against 100.0 and perplexity on novel tokens 2.65 % higher [-0.02 %, +4.93 %]. On three 8 to 9B reference models, at the same split and tail as the identity fill, the fitted map retrieves 49.1 and 49.6 more filled-region RULER points on the two dense models (at that split Llama's loss is worse), and its long-document loss is +/-0.03 nats of the released SwiftKV checkpoint's.
comment: 50 pages, 15 figures, 38 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/Approximate-Science/ridgefill-data

title: ICare-DT: a digital twin for continuous forecasting of intensive care patients
summary: Digital twins of intensive care patients should update forecasts from new data and predict treatment responses, but few studies test whether routine records support either.
