title: Coreset-Induced Conditional Velocity Flow Matching
comments: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 48 pages. Code: https://github.com/ziwaa-se/CCVFM
summary: We propose Coreset-Induced Conditional Velocity Flow Matching (CCVFM), a generative model that augments hierarchical rectified flow with a data-informed source distribution. Standard flow matching regresses only the conditional mean of the velocity; hierarchical flow matching instead models the full conditional velocity law with a second, inner flow in velocity space, but this inner flow is asked to transport isotropic Gaussian noise to a multimodal target velocity distribution from scratch. Our key observation is that this inner source can be replaced by a closed-form surrogate built from a coreset of the target. CCVFM first compresses the target into weighted atoms using an entropic Sinkhorn coreset and lifts them to a Gaussian mixture. The induced conditional velocity law is then a closed-form Gaussian mixture that can be sampled without a learned neural sampler. A lightweight correction flow, trained from this surrogate source, then refines the remaining surrogate-to-target residual rather than learning an entire noise-to-data map. We prove that the surrogate transport cost equals the target-surrogate Wasserstein gap under an explicit compression assumption, whereas the noise-source analogue has a dimension-scale lower bound. We further characterize the conditional second moment of the training target when the source velocity is drawn from the surrogate law independently of the target velocity, and show that the part of it that depends on the source is small when the surrogate conditional law is close to the true conditional velocity law in mean and covariance. Empirically, on MNIST, CIFAR-10, ImageNet-32, and CelebA-HQ, the proposed method reaches competitive few-step generation under matched architectures. Code is available at https://github.com/ziwaa-se/CCVFM.
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 48 pages. Code: https://github.com/ziwaa-se/CCVFM

title: Training-Free Generative Sampling via Moment-Matched Score Smoothing
summary: Diffusion models generate samples by denoising along the score of a perturbed target distribution. In practice, one trains a neural diffusion model, which is computationally expensive. Recent work suggests that score matching implicitly smooths the empirical score, and that this smoothing bias promotes generalization by capturing low-dimensional data geometry. We propose moment-matched score-smoothed overdamped Langevin dynamics (MM-SOLD), a training-free interacting particle sampler that enforces the target moments throughout the sampling trajectory. We prove that the one-particle marginal of the ideal constrained Gibbs equilibrium converges, as the number of particles grows, to a Gibbs--Boltzmann density obtained by exponentially tilting the naive score-smoothed target. Its mean and covariance match the training GMM, even for rank-deficient data. We additionally establish sampling consistency, statistical target-error bounds for bounded data, and consistency of a safeguarded BAOAB-based tilting estimator. Experiments on 2D distributions and latent-space image generation show that MM-SOLD enables fast, robust, latent sampling on CPUs using fixed pretrained autoencoders, with sample fidelity and diversity competitive with neural diffusion baselines.

title: Self-Distillation is Optimal Among Spectral Shrinkage Estimators
summary: Self-distillation has emerged as a promising technique for improving model performance in modern machine learning systems. We develop the statistical foundations of self-distillation in high-dimensional linear regression by introducing and analyzing a broad class of estimators, namely spectral shrinkage estimators. We consider both spiked and general covariance matrices. For the former, we establish that when the covariance has $s$ distinct spikes, $s$-step self-distillation achieves optimal prediction among spectral shrinkage estimators, outperforming well-known estimators in statistics and machine learning. Moreover, we show that $s$ steps are necessary for optimality: any $(s-k)$-step distilled estimator is strictly suboptimal for $1 \leq k \leq s$. For general covariance matrices, we show that self-distillation approaches the optimal limiting prediction risk among continuous spectral shrinkage estimators as the number of distillation steps increases. We further develop a generalized cross-validation procedure for selecting the distillation parameters from data and establish an asymptotic oracle guarantee for the resulting estimator. We also study a federated approach where multiple data centers share spectral shrinkage estimators and a common server seeks to aggregate them to achieve optimal performance. In this case, we find that the best local rule again takes the form of self-distillation, though it differs from the optimal rule when data are hosted centrally on a single server. Together, our results explain why self-distillation improves predictive performance and provide a broader statistical framework that connects it to classical shrinkage-based methods.

title: Optimizing Computational-Statistical Runtime for Wasserstein Distance Estimation
summary: Squared Wasserstein distance is a frequently used tool to measure discrepancy between probability distributions. This distance is typically computed between empirical measures of size $n$ from two underlying random samples. Unfortunately, even in lower dimensional Euclidean space problems $\left( d \in \{2,3\} \right)$, algorithms for Wasserstein distance computation with approximate or exact precision guarantees scale poorly in the runtime as a function of $n$ and the desired precision. In response, we consider the computational-statistical runtime, where the goal is to estimate from samples the Wasserstein distance between potentially smooth measures up to $ε$-additive error in expectation with respect to the sampling; we allow $O(1)$ computational cost for collecting a sample. Towards this, we develop a Sample-Sketch-Solve paradigm where we introduce a regular cartesian grid sketch of the samples. We show that (especially under $α$-Hölder smooth distributions) this can compress the data without increasing asymptotic error, and also regularizes the structure which enables faster exact algorithms. Ultimately, we approximate $W_2^2(P,Q)$ within $ε$ error in $ε^{-\max(2,\frac{d+1+o(1)}{1+α})}$ time for $0 < α< 1$ Hölder smooth distributions $P,Q$ on $(0,1)^{d}$; an optimal $Θ(ε^{-2})$ for $α> 1/2$ when $d=2$ and nearly optimal as $α\to 1$ when $d = 3$.

title: Platonic Representations in the Human Brain: Unsupervised Recovery of Universal Geometry
summary: The Strong Platonic Representation Hypothesis suggests that representational convergence in artificial neural networks can be harnessed constructively: embeddings can be translated across models through a universal latent space without paired data. We ask whether an analogous geometry can be recovered across human brains. Using fMRI data from the Natural Scenes Dataset, we propose a self-supervised encoder that learns subject-specific embeddings from brain data alone by exploiting repeated stimulus presentations. We show that these independently learned spaces can be translated across subjects using unsupervised orthogonal rotations, without paired cross-subject samples or intermediate model representations. Synchronizing pairwise rotations into a single shared latent space further improves cross-subject retrieval. These results provide evidence for a shared geometry in learned representations of human visual responses: subject-specific fMRI embeddings can be aligned across individuals within a common coordinate system.

title: Action-BED: Task-Driven Bayesian Experimental Design with Singly Intractable Objectives
comments: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Camera-ready version; revised presentation, additional experiments, and corrected references
summary: Bayesian experimental design (BED) has traditionally been based on maximising expected uncertainty reductions from prior to posterior. A major shortfall of this approach is that it leads to doubly intractable objectives that are difficult to optimise, while customising them to particular downstream tasks of interest can also be difficult. Following first principles decision theory, we demonstrate that BED can alternatively be formulated in terms of an expected future loss (EFL) on downstream actions, providing a simple and naturally task-driven framework. Critically, we then show that all such EFLs can be rearranged into singly intractable objectives that can be jointly optimised with respect to both the design policy and a downstream action policy using stochastic gradients, an approach we refer to as ACTION-BED. This formulation further sidesteps the need for any explicit posterior or marginal likelihood estimation and is naturally implicit, requiring only the ability to sample from the joint model over model parameters and data, and evaluate the downstream loss function. It thus allows design policies to be learned more effectively, efficiently, and simply than existing methods, while providing easy customisation to different downstream tasks and losses.
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Camera-ready version; revised presentation, additional experiments, and corrected references

title: SGD Provably Prioritizes a Shortcut Spurious Feature in the XOR Model
summary: Neural networks are known to be susceptible to over-reliance on spurious correlations. However, the precise mechanism by which models exploit shortcut features is not fully understood, and algorithms to mitigate this behavior rely on as yet unjustified assumptions about the learned representations. In this work, we provide the first end-to-end theoretical characterization of spurious feature learning for two-layer ReLU neural networks trained by online minibatch SGD on the logistic loss. We consider data drawn from the high-dimensional Boolean hypercube with a quadratic signal function (namely XOR) and a linear spurious correlation. We show that SGD learns the spurious feature first, and exponentially fast. Moreover, the optimization dynamics couple the spurious and signal features, with a stronger spurious component inhibiting signal feature learning. Our analysis reveals precise phase transitions in the learning dynamics. In the first phase, alignment between the signs of the spurious feature and second-layer weight drives rapid growth of the spurious feature. In the second phase, large majority group margin slows learning and the signal feature remains suppressed. When the spurious correlation is maximally strong, we show theoretically that the spurious feature dominates even at the sample complexity threshold where XOR would be learned in isolation (i.e., if the spurious feature was absent). In contrast, when the correlation strength is constant, we provide preliminary evidence that the model can eventually learn the XOR signal, although the spurious feature is not forgotten.

title: Unconditional Unclonable Encryption
summary:
We give an unconditional construction of information-theoretically secure one-time private-key unclonable encryption for one-bit messages, with efficient encryption and decryption and exponentially small unclonable-indistinguishability advantage. Previous work by Bhattacharyya and Culf (Nature Physics, 2026) and Bhattacharyya, Broadbent, and Culf (arXiv:2603.08916) either only showed inverse-polynomial security loss or required inefficient encryption/decryption operations; we avoid both of these caveats.
  Our scheme's key is a uniformly random non-identity phase-free Pauli on $n$ qubits, and bit $a$ is encrypted as a random $(-1)^a$ eigenstate of that Pauli. We prove that the probability that both receivers recover the bit is at most $1/2 + O\left(2^{-n/2}\right).$ By a lower bound due to Broadbent, Culf, and Rochette (IACR Communications in Cryptology, 2026), this is the best probability bound achievable with $n$-qubit ciphertexts while ensuring perfect correctness (up to the constant hidden in the $O(\cdot)$).

title: Model-Agnostic FDR Control via Group Gaussian Mirror and Permutation SHAP
summary: Most FDR-controlled feature selection methods are designed for coordinate-wise hypotheses, where each feature has a single weight or importance score. This abstraction fails in sequential and grouped models, where one original feature is represented by a block of sub-features, such as lags, recurrent states, or attention-based interactions. We propose a grouped-feature FDR control framework for such settings. For grouped linear models, we construct null-symmetric block-level mirror statistics with matrix-valued perturbations. For neural sequential models, we combine Permutation SHAP derivatives as model-agnostic block-level importance scores with kernel-based dependence measure. The framework is model-agnostic across network architectures, does not require specifying the covariate distribution, and reduces to Gaussian Mirror or Neural Gaussian Mirror when the block size is one. We prove FDR control for low- and high-dimensional grouped linear models and asymptotic symmetry of smoothed Permutation SHAP derivatives under fixed fitted nonlinear models. Experiments on simulated and real-world datasets show reliable FDR control and improved power under correlated grouped-feature signals.

title: Guidance for Prior Change via Density Ratio Estimation
summary: Simulation-Based Inference (SBI) serves as a vital framework for parameter inference in scientific fields where simulators involve intractable likelihoods, yet while amortized generative models offer rapid posterior estimation, they are often restricted by the specific priors used during training, thereby limiting their flexibility as prior knowledge evolves. To address this prior dependency, PriorGuide was introduced as an inference-time guidance method, but due to its intractable formulation, it relies on Gaussian approximations of the reverse transition kernel and Gaussian mixture model fitting for the prior ratio, both of which introduce systematic bias. Motivated by these limitations, we propose an unbiased test-time guidance framework that leverages Density Ratio Estimation (DRE) to learn a score guidance term, effectively decoupling the inference process from the prior training. Moreover, our framework remains agnostic to the specific density ratio estimators, making it a general and flexible framework for handling prior changes. Experimental results across multiple tasks demonstrate that our method matches or outperforms PriorGuide on C2ST and MMD in most tasks while maintaining robustness even under limited overlap between the training and target priors. Furthermore, we apply our method to Bayesian updating for parameter inference from planetary light-curve data, where it also demonstrates strong effectiveness and robustness. Code is available at https://github.com/a-chenchen/dre-based-prior-guidance .

title: Finding and using interpretable latents in a neutrino foundation model with sparse autoencoders
summary: We present a first application of sparse-autoencoder-based mechanistic interpretability to particle physics. Studying a neutrino foundation model pretrained on IceCube data and fine-tuned for direction reconstruction, we identify a validated atlas of physical concepts in the model representation, using a strict validation protocol consisting of held-out tests, matched nuisance controls, and replication across independent dictionary trainings. Causal interventions show that the direction head barely draws on this atlas. Motivated by this underused information, we train an uncertainty head on the same event-level representation to predict the model's angular reconstruction error. Unlike the direction head, it depends causally on quality and brightness features from the atlas. These results suggest that mechanistic interpretability can reveal learned latent physics encoded within a model's internal representation and help design downstream tasks that exploit it.

title: Amortized Score-Hamiltonian Policy Iteration: A Grid-Free Scheme for Relaxed Stochastic Control Problems
summary: We develop an amortized, grid-free implementation of continuous Langevin dynamics based policy-value iteration for entropy-regularized, infinite-horizon relaxed stochastic control problems. The improvement rate of the exact iteration is a discounted aggregate of relative Fisher information between the policy and the Gibbs law of its Hamiltonian. The associated score residual is the velocity with which the control's Langevin dynamics transport its law. We project this velocity onto a conditional sampler shared across states, instead of one Langevin dynamics per state, and the value dynamics onto a parametric critic, estimating both projections at sampled states to obtain coupled actor--critic flows. The score loss measures the actor's agreement with the current critic, while the policy-evaluation residual measures the critic's agreement with the actor. We also derive gradient and Hessian residuals, including a Feynman--Kac representation for the gradient equation, to control errors not detected by the projected value iteration. An exact decomposition of the HJB residual combines these errors into a policy-suboptimality bound under verification and logarithmic Sobolev assumptions. In the linear-quadratic class, both projections are exact and recover the pointwise iteration, and we provide numerical experiments on general models to demonstrate the coupled actor--critic learning in high-dimensions.

title: Adaptive Variance Reduction across Smoothness and Noise Conditions
summary:
In this paper, we study adaptive stochastic non-convex optimization under unknown smoothness and noise conditions. Our algorithms require no smoothness constant, noise bound, initial function gap, or oracle-regime label. We first propose a fixed-budget method that combines normalized momentum, recursive variance reduction, and a fresh gradient stage, followed by fresh validation of the candidates. We prove that the same output has expected gradient norm $O(T^{-1/4})$ under objective smoothness and bounded noise variance, $O(T^{-1/3})$ under average smoothness, and $O(T^{-1/2})$ for noiseless gradients, where $T$ counts individual gradient evaluations.
  We then develop an anytime algorithm whose three optimization paths preserve their endpoints across reporting and budget-extension boundaries. The same three rates hold at every deterministic query budget, although the algorithm receives no information about the budget $T$. The analysis combines a scale potential, a uniform second-moment bound, and accounting for candidates retained through unfinished blocks. An optional sample-mean selector further reduces cumulative validation work from $O(T)$ to $O(T^{2/3})$ while preserving these rates.

title: Defense Filters for Robust Learning of Partially Observed Dynamical Systems
summary: Robust estimation of unknown system dynamics from partial observations under attack is a core challenge in learning for control, increasingly critical in multi-agent networks subject to adversarial data poisoning. Existing methods either require highly restrictive assumptions on the adversary or yield weak error bounds. In this paper, we consider identifying partially observed linear dynamical systems subject to adversarial attacks with an attack probability $p < 0.5$ at each time. We propose a defense-filtering framework leveraging knowledge of the observation matrix to construct a defense filter satisfying full column rank and subspace separability conditions, which enables the evaluation of a single-attack scenario against observed data. Using this framework, we analyze the constrained $\ell_2$-norm estimator and establish finite-sample error bounds for recovering the Markov parameter matrix up to a linear transformation. This is the first approach to provide provable system identification guarantees via a defense filter for partially observed systems subject to harsh environments where the attack probability approaches $0.5$.

title: On Multi-label radio Labelings of Graphs
summary: We propose and study a multi-labeling generalization of the $k$-radio labeling problem of graphs: given a graph $G$ and integers $k$ and $m$, assign to each vertex of $G$ a set of $m$ integer labels such that distinct labels assigned to a vertex differ by at least $k+1$, and the labels of any two distinct vertices $x$ and $y$ pairwise differ by at least $k+1-d(x,y)$, with $d(x,y)$ being the distance between vertices $x$ and $y$. We prove general bounds on the minimum span of such a labeling and more refined results for the case $k=1$. For paths and cycles, we derive sharp bounds on the minimum span when $k$ is small. We finally propose a conjecture for the minimum span on the path and for an almost-tight bound on the cycle.

title: Integrate the Reward, Don't Sample It: Window Likelihood for Interruptions and Backchannels in Full-Duplex Speech Models
summary: When a user talks over a full-duplex spoken dialogue model, the model must decide whether the user is interrupting (stop) or only backchannelling (carry on). Post-training can make the model better at telling the two apart, or merely change how readily it stops. The whole-rollout GRPO runs we examine never lower both error rates: any gain in discrimination is offset by a threshold shift, and two released checkpoints discriminate no better. We trace this partly to how the reward is used. The probability that the model stops inside a short window is a known function of a few stop probabilities that the policy itself emits, yet GRPO estimates it by sampling. A window on which all rollouts agree then gives that update no gradient, even when all fail, and whole-rollout credit reaches decisions the reward never judges. Window likelihood (WL) instead samples a continuation and integrates over its stop decisions: the probability of the correct outcome is computed in closed form and its logarithm maximised. On HumDial-FDBench, across four open models with different stop interfaces, WL gives the best F1 and lowers both error rates beyond their confidence intervals, which no GRPO run does, without adding talking into silence.

title: Finite Fields: Root Sets, Frobenius, and Algebraic Structure
summary: This monograph develops finite field theory through root sets, Frobenius orbits, trace duality, and cyclic modules, with applications to polynomial constructions and algebraic coding theory. Root-set descent and linearized polynomials connect field extensions, normal bases, invariant subspaces, and linear recurrences. Cyclotomic cosets link additive symmetries and local phase data with polynomial composition, factorization, and compatible lifting. Low-degree subfield representations and relative traces lead to root-block recovery, while return maps on root fibers organize constructions of irreducible polynomials. Coding applications include duality, distance bounds, Fourier support, and syndrome decoding. Character sums yield trace-norm distributions, the primitive normal basis theorem, and recurrences for extension-field sums and curve point counts. The final chapter constructs finite fields as residue fields of unramified p-adic extensions and relates Teichmuller representatives and Hensel lifting to cyclotomic orbits, periodic digit expansions, Witt carries, coefficient valuations, and Newton slopes. The emphasis throughout is on explicit proofs and reusable connections between field structure, orbit structure, and linear dependence.

title: Classification Aggregation with Multiple Memberships
summary: People face the problem of classifying objects into categories while aggregating their opinions. We axiomatically study such a classification aggregation problem with multiple memberships, meaning that each individual assigns one category to every object, whereas the resulting classification may assign more than one category. Under the natural settings and axioms (i.e., Independence and Supportiveness), each of our new axioms -- Responsibility, Split Stability and Rejection Stability -- characterises what we call the junta rules. The rules assign a category to an object exactly when some member of a fixed coalition does so. The coalitions that can secure an assignment form a grill, a topological structure implied by an ultrafilter. Hence, the study parallels the literature on Arrow's theorem characterised by the decisive coalition structures. An infinite population setting is also investigated to clarify the differences among the axioms.

title: A Novel Conditional Adversarial Diffusion Model for High-Fidelity OCT-to-OCT Image Translation and Precise Anti-VEGF Therapy Response Prediction in Diabetic Macular Edema
comments: 18 pages, 8 figures, 6 tables, Submitted to IEEE Journal of Biomedical and Health Informatics
summary: Diabetic macular edema (DME) is a leading cause of severe vision loss among working-age adults. Although intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) injections currently serve as the first-line therapy for DME, a notable subset of patients fails to respond despite the substantial cost and clinical burden, suggesting they may benefit more from alternative interventions. Automated, noninvasive pre-treatment response assessment could therefore spare non-responders from the current trial-and-error treatment paradigm. In this study, we propose a novel conditional adversarial diffusion framework that synthesizes post-treatment optical coherence tomography (OCT) images from baseline scans, enabling the derivation of each patient's initial response to anti-VEGF therapy. The model was developed with subject-level 5-fold cross-validation on a US cohort (n = 127) and externally validated on an independent Iranian cohort (n = 44). Benchmarked against fourteen baseline and state-of-the-art translation models, the proposed model achieved the best treatment-response prediction performance among the methods evaluated for that task on both cohorts, with balanced accuracies of 85.7% and 93.0% on the US cohort and 85.2% and 95.3% on the external Iranian cohort at the 10% and 20% central subfield thickness reduction thresholds, respectively. Ultimately, this framework offers a decision-support tool to help ophthalmologists anticipate initial anti-VEGF outcomes in DME prior to treatment initiation, toward personalized therapy selection. The source code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.
comment: 18 pages, 8 figures, 6 tables, Submitted to IEEE Journal of Biomedical and Health Informatics

title: Descending Everest, Part II: Oracle Complexity of Minimizing a Sum of Convex $(L_0,L_1)$-Smooth Functions
comments: 57 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables, 5 algorithms. Second paper in the Descending Everest series; Part I: arXiv:2610.21461
summary: We study the minimization of the average of $n$ convex $(L_0,L_1)$-smooth functions: the Hessian norm of each function is bounded by an affine function of its gradient norm. We assume known upper bounds $R$ on the distance from the starting point to a minimizer and $δ$ on the difference between the minimum of the average and the average of the infima of the components. We derive upper and lower bounds on the oracle complexity of reaching accuracy $\varepsilon$ in function value in expectation. Up to logarithmic factors, both bounds are of order $n(1+(L_1R)^{2/3}) +\sqrt{\frac{n(L_0+L_1^2δ)R^2}{\varepsilon}+n(L_1R)^2}$. The upper bound is attained by the proposed method YETI. The method combines ideas of accelerated proximal methods and variance reduction methods with a heuristic for choosing additional points. The number of oracle calls made by the heuristic is bounded, which preserves the upper bound on the total number of queries needed to reach the target accuracy. In the experiments, YETI is compared with first-order methods on synthetic problems and Poisson regression problems. We also examine the stopping criterion and the effect of the heuristic separately. The lower bound is obtained by an explicit construction of families of instances that are hard for any first-order method.
comment: 57 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables, 5 algorithms. Second paper in the Descending Everest series; Part I: arXiv:2610.21461

title: Oscillatory Phase Coding Emerges in Adaptive RNNs for Flexible Working Memory
summary: Oscillatory phase coding (OPC) is widely observed in neural systems and has been implicated in cognitive functions such as memory and sequence processing. However, its computational role and neural substrates remain largely unclear. Here, we studied OPC by training recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with adaptation to perform sequence working memory tasks with variable delays. After training, we found that OPC emerges in the RNN spontaneously: the memorized items recur at distinct phases of a shared rhythm, with oscillation amplitude encoding item identity and phase encoding serial order. Ablation studies identified three key elements required for OPC: adaptation in neural dynamics, variable delay in memory retention, and flexibility in reading out information. Neuron-type analysis revealed the emergence of content and time cells in the trained RNN, and they process item identity and sequence order separately. Recurrent connectivity analysis revealed phase-organized connections among time cells and structured connections within digit-selective content-cell groups. Inspired by these findings, we proposed a neural circuit model which reproduces OPC through interactions between content units and an adaptive time ring. Together, this study reveals how OPC arises from network structures and task demands, offers insights into the implementation and computational mechanisms of OPC in biological systems, and inspires us to develop computational models for human-like cognitive functions.

title: Arctic-SAR: A Cross-Sensor RADARSAT Constellation Mission and Sentinel-1 Dataset and Fusion Benchmark for Multi-Task Sea Ice Mapping
summary: Current sea ice mapping benchmarks are mostly built around single-sensor SAR products, limiting the evaluation of cross-sensor variability and the effectiveness of combining observations from different SAR platforms. Models trained on such datasets may also be sensitive to sensor-specific artifacts, radiometric characteristics, and acquisition conditions, which can reduce robustness and limit generalization. To address these limitations, this study introduces Arctic-SAR, a cross-sensor SAR dataset for Arctic sea ice mapping, constructed by matching RADARSAT Constellation Mission (RCM) dual-polarization imagery with Sentinel-1 scenes from the AI4Arctic Sea Ice Dataset. The dataset consists of 221 co-registered scenes and supports multi-task prediction of sea ice concentration (SIC), stage of development (SOD), and floe size (FLOE). In addition to the dataset, we establish a benchmark for cross-sensor SAR sea ice mapping by quantifying the contribution of RCM imagery and evaluating single-sensor baselines alongside representative input-, feature-, and decision-level fusion strategies within a consistent multi-task U-Net framework. Across three independent runs, the test results show that the effectiveness of cross-sensor fusion is strongly dependent on the fusion strategy and prediction task. Decision-level fusion achieves the highest mean combined score of $77.28\pm0.29\%$, essentially matching the Sentinel-1-only baseline at $77.26\pm0.13\%$, while achieving the highest SIC \(R^2\) score. These findings show that Sentinel-1 and RCM provide task- and class-dependent information, but that simple joint cross-sensor fusion does not consistently improve generalization over a strong single-sensor baseline. Arctic-SAR therefore provides a benchmark for cross-sensor SAR fusion research in automated Arctic sea ice mapping.

title: Destructive augmentations for prostate lesion segmentation on heterogeneous biparametric MRI data
summary:
Training prostate lesion segmentation models on biparametric MRI (bpMRI) is limited by small datasets with heterogeneous imaging acquisition protocols and annotations. In this work, we train a segmentation model on a combined cohort of 1,579 lesion-containing training cases from five datasets, representing, to our knowledge, the largest collection of prostate lesion annotations used for this task.
  Additionally, we investigate two complementary improvements to the widely used nnU-Net framework. First, we introduce a random wavelet augmentation and show that random sym4 (Symlet) wavelets outperform random convolution augmentation in terms of average Dice score, with only a modest reduction in F1 score due to lower precision. Second, we evaluate instance-level losses and show that Connected-Component-based Dice (CC-Dice)-CE loss complements BackSplit, yielding better performance than BackSplit alone.
  Together, these improvements achieve the best overall performance, reaching a Dice score of 0.614 on the public Prostate158 test set and establishing a new state-of-the-art on this benchmark.
  We publicly release our training code and model weights.

title: SideAge-RiskNet: Predicted Mammographic-Age Features for Future Breast Cancer Risk and Laterality Prediction
summary: Whether breast-specific mammographic aging provides information beyond chronological age for future cancer prediction remains unclear. We propose SideAge-RiskNet, a framework integrating predicted mammographic-age features with breast-specific representations for multi-year breast cancer risk and conditional laterality prediction. A side-aware DenseNet121 trained on never-cancer reference examinations estimates left and right breast ages. Age-adjusted residuals and bilateral age descriptors are subsequently fused with corresponding image representations, while clinical variables contribute through an image--clinical risk branch. The framework jointly predicts cumulative cancer risk over 1--5 years and the subsequently affected breast among unilateral cancer cases. Across 4,480 EMBED and 248 external examinations, pre-cancer scans demonstrated pronounced bilateral age asymmetry. SideAge-RiskNet established state-of-the-art performance in 1--5-year risk assessment over Mirai and AsymMirai with mean risk AUROCs of 81.73% on EMBED and 72.83% on CSMC. Furthermore, it enabled conditional cancer laterality prediction, achieving AUROCs of 73.26% and 82.53%, respectively. This demonstrates the critical utility of bilateral aging phenotypes in localized breast cancer risk surveillance.

title: CNVAE: Anatomically Correct Segmentation via Conditional Generative Modeling
summary: Supervised deep learning segmentation models, although unparalleled in performance, are not immune to anatomical mistakes. We develop a segmentation-by-generation paradigm extending the Nouveau VAE (NVAE) generative framework for anatomically correct cardiac segmentation. In particular, we propose a novel conditional NVAE model (CNVAE) for conditional shape generation, and explore its capabilities for image segmentation in two scenarios: (1) direct image-to-mask CNVAE for one-step segmentation; (2) mask-to-mask CNVAE for refinement of segmentation masks produced by third-party segmentation models. Both models are lightweight and return consistently anatomically valid segmentation masks (> 98% success rate, an improvement of 15% above state-of-the-art segmentation models) on the cardiac segmentation/editing tasks of interest, without loss of accuracy in segmented contours.

title: Volumetric Latent Diffusion for Brain Tumour Segmentation with Missing Modalities
summary: Brain tumour segmentation from magnetic resonance imaging normally assumes that all four imaging sequences are available, but in clinical practice one or more are frequently missing. Existing methods for incomplete inputs learn modality-invariant representations or distil from a full-modality teacher, and return a single deterministic mask. Gen- erative formulations instead model a distribution over plausible masks, but the cost of sampling at full resolution has largely confined them to two dimensions. This paper proposes a three-dimensional conditional latent diffusion framework for whole-tumour segmentation from incom- plete multi-sequence MRI. Images and annotations are first compressed by two volumetric autoencoders, which makes diffusion over whole vol- umes affordable, and sequences are dropped at random during training so that a single model handles every combination of missing sequences. Because the model samples rather than predicts, repeated draws also yield a voxel-wise map of disagreement at no extra training cost. Evalu- ations on 2,601 studies from BraTS 2023 and 2024 show that the method reaches 0.955 Dice with all four sequences and 0.904 with FLAIR alone, and that it is the most accurate of the four methods compared in eight of the fifteen configurations. The disagreement between draws widens as sequences are withheld, giving a signal that accompanies the prediction rather than replacing it

title: RapidMitDet: Boosting Computational Efficiency for Mitosis Detection via Magnification Alignment
summary: Automated mitosis detection is a critical research focus, enabling pathologists to rapidly assess mitotic indices for tumor malignancy evaluation. However, most of the existing detection approaches suffer from significant computational inefficiency due to the giga-pixel image resolution of Whole-Slide Images (WSIs), which greatly hinders their clinical applicability. In this study, we propose RapidMitDet, a computational efficient mitosis detection approach. Our method employs a coarse-to-fine framework, first identifying mitotic candidates at lower magnification and then confirming them at higher magnification. In the coarse-detection stage, we introduce magnification-aligned knowledge distillation to reduce the information gap between magnification levels while minimizing the performance degradation in the lower magnification detection model. In the subsequent fine-classification stage, we propose adaptive triplet learning (ATL) to optimize infomative sample selection, thereby enhancing discrimination between mitotic and non-mitotic instances. Experimental results show that RapidMitDet achieves the optimal accuracy-efficiency balance at 20x magnification, improving computational speed by up to 5.62 times over the latest state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods. Due to its lightweight model design, RapidMitDet can also deliver efficient detection at higher magnification (40x) while achieving even higher detection performance. In WSI-level evaluations, our method shows strong agreement with pathologists' diagnoses (ICCs: 0.879 (40x), 0.822 (20x)) while maintaining superior efficiency, highlighting its potential for clinical application. Code is available at https://github.com/logincat/RapidMitDet

title: Physical Sensing Verification for Cognitive ISAC against UAV Spoofing via Digital Twins
summary: As integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) lets 5G and 6G base stations detect drones, software agents will soon act on what they sense. This amplifies the threat of a relay replaying the base station's signal as a phantom drone. For such cognitive ISAC systems, this paper proposes a wall-based physical check. A digital twin (DT) predicts where a real target's wall echo must arrive; a relay can fake range, but not where its own reflections come from. The paper proves that line-of-sight beam steering cannot expose a matched relay, and that, under stated conditions, a single-antenna relay faking a wall echo leaves a telltale echo where a genuine target leaves none. In a pre-registered ray-tracing study, the twin's evidence separated genuine targets from replays perfectly (AUC 1.000) on held-out streets, and a later-registered passive check needing no extra transmission accepted every genuine target and no replay. The primary active probe was inconclusive, at 5.3\% false acceptances against a 5\% limit, for lack of threshold margin. At the evaluated relay positions, the conditional bound certifies 3 of 24 held-out streets, reproduced on fresh ones, against single-antenna relay signals meeting its conditions, adaptive or fixed, and 11 of 24 at double bandwidth.

title: Conflict-Aware Meta-Learning for Generalizable Speech Deepfake Detection
summary: Speech deepfake detectors built on large self-supervised learning front-ends achieve high in-domain accuracy, yet suffer degradation under domain shift caused by unseen synthesizers, transmission codecs, or unfamiliar acoustic conditions. Meta-learning, particularly model-agnostic meta-learning for domain generalization (MLDG), addresses this issue by simulating domain shifts. However, applying MLDG directly introduces a bi-level optimization challenge that remains unsolved. First, effective domain-shift emulation requires genuine distributional gaps between meta-splits, yet such gaps can frequently produce gradient conflicts, destabilizing the bi-level optimization. Second, the stochastic nature of mini-batch gradients causes the reference direction to fluctuate across iterations, resulting in an optimization trajectory that fails to achieve domain generalization. We propose a conflict-aware meta-learning (CAML) framework, which addresses both challenges through three complementary components. Firstly, base domain gradient surgery (base-DGS) introduces an asymmetric projection that treats the meta-train gradient as a primary anchor. Secondly, EMA-DGS replaces the unstable anchor with its exponential moving average (EMA), providing a stable optimization trajectory anchor that substantially reduces domain-shift-induced conflict detections. Thirdly, layer-wise DGS (LW-DGS) further extends the framework to individual parameter tensors, enabling fine-grained, layer-specific intervention that targets conflict-prone layers while leaving well-aligned parameters intact. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed CAML framework achieves lower EER than the compared baselines on most cross-dataset evaluations across multiple cross-dataset benchmarks and architectures, achieving a maximum relative improvement of 45.2% in terms of EER.

title: 13,000-Fold Frequency Down Conversion From 280 MHz to 21 kHz Using Mechanical Frequency Combs
summary: Optical frequency combs bridge the microwave and terahertz regimes by down-converting terahertz optical energy into microwave signals. A photodetector converts the comb's equally spaced lines, generated through optical nonlinearities, into a low-frequency tone at their spacing. Here, we present the first mechanical version of this process, using mechanical frequency combs to downconvert energy over 4 orders of magnitude, from the MHz to kHz regime. Thin-film lithium niobate (LN) is used to design an acoustic resonator with a wide range of mode frequencies. We achieve phononic comb excitation from 250 MHz to 900 MHz and compare the electrical and laser Doppler vibrometer (LDV) measurements at 277 MHz. We then show the low-frequency spectrum of the devices, highlighting mechanical motion at the comb's spacing and demonstrating energy transfer from 277 MHz to 21 kHz.

title: Energy-Aware Vertically Layered Pinching-Antenna System Design with Probabilistic LoS Availability
summary: This paper investigates a vertically layered pinching antenna (PA) system, in which dielectric waveguides deployed at different heights provide additional vertical spatial degrees of freedom for line-of-sight (LoS)-favorable PA placement. We consider a practical energy model that captures in-waveguide attenuation, base station-to-feed-point optical-fiber loss, and PA repositioning energy, along with a statistical LoS-availability model that depends on elevation and distance. We then jointly optimize the transmit beamforming, PA positions, time allocation, and transmission rates to maximize the expected successfully delivered frame-effective sum rate under per-user outage and quality-of-service constraints. To avoid enumerating the exponentially many LoS states, we derive a certified conditional-moment outage envelope for outage-guaranteed rate selection and a differentiable safe approximation of the chance constraints to facilitate tractable optimization. Building on these results, a block coordinate descent algorithm with a penalty-aided majorization-minimization procedure attains a high-quality suboptimal solution. Simulation results confirm the gains of vertical layering and reveal a fundamental energy-LoS tradeoff: LoS-favorable PA placement generally enhances both performance and reliability, although it incurs higher attenuation, path loss, and energy costs.

title: Stochastic High-Resolution Parameter-Based Channel Modeling for Sub-Terahertz Outdoor Device-to-Device Propagation at 145 GHz
comments: Currently under submitted and under revision in the IEEE Transactions on Wireless Communications
summary: Since device-to-device (D2D) systems operating in the sub-THz regime are of interest for a variety of 6G applications, modeling their propagation channels is therefore essential. This paper presents high-resolution parameter estimation (HRPE) of specular multipath components (MPCs) as well as diffuse multipath components (DMCs) from an extensive measurement campaign. The extracted MPCs and DMCs are then clustered, and statistical models for both intra- and inter-cluster statistics are established. Among other insights, we find a large number (typically 10-50) of clusters; both the powers and densities of MPCs within each cluster show significant variations. DMC occurs both when associated with discrete MPCs and standalone. The paper provides a complete model that can generate double-directional impulse responses, and a MATLAB program implementing it is made available. Extensive verifications of "derived" (not directly modeled) parameters are provided as well.
comment: Currently under submitted and under revision in the IEEE Transactions on Wireless Communications

title: Quantifying System-Level Performance Bottlenecks in Hyperspectral Target Detection
summary: Discerning core performance bottlenecks in hyperspectral target detection is highly challenging given the complex interplay between sub-systems of the imaging chain (scene, atmosphere, sensor and processing). Prior sensitivity and limitation studies offer narrow insights applicable to specific system configurations. To address the need for broader generalization, an analysis framework was constructed to quantify limitations from large ensembles of model scenarios. Key components of the framework include the use of canonical scene representations and the log-weighted area under the ROC curve (wAUC), a metric well-suited for rare target detection. By analyzing thousands of scenarios, parametric thresholds were quantified where detection performance degrades, corresponding to "knees" in performance curves. A knee significance score (KSS) is introduced to assess the relative importance of these thresholds. The framework an airborne VNIR sensor implanted in 28,000 scenarios using seven system parameters spanning the scene, atmosphere and sensor. Results suggest that aerosol visibility in the 2-6 km range is the dominant limiter in detection, followed by subpixel target percentages of 15-35%, and background clutter modeled using a t-distribution with 3-5 degrees of freedom.

title: AccentCanvas: Activity-Guided Bidirectional Accent Conversion
summary: Accent conversion for dubbing must change pronunciation while preserving content, voice, and source timing. Normalization alone cannot produce requested non-native accents, and matching total duration does not ensure local speech/pause alignment. We present AccentCanvas, a shared discrete diffusion model for normalization and L1-to-L2 conversion, trained on cross-paired shared-prompt recordings and synthetic pairs. Frame-level speech activity and repetition-preserving units guide local timing through synthesis. Across both tasks, AccentCanvas achieves the highest accent conversion performance (Accent Arrival) and mean listener-rated accent similarity among compared systems, with over 73% lower speech-boundary error than the best baseline for each task. These gains accompany higher L1-to-L2 WER than TokAN and Vevo-Style, highlighting a tradeoff between requested-accent resemblance and ASR-based content recognition. https://smokedindia.github.io/accentcanvas/

title: DeepRT-Cal: Learning to Calibrate Ray-Traced Twin Channel Statistics with Low-Fidelity Environmental Geometry
summary: Sixth-generation (6G) wireless systems increasingly rely on digital twin channels (DTCs) to represent and interact with physical radio environments. Ray tracing (RT) is naturally suited to DTC construction because it provides deterministic and physically interpretable channel predictions. However, high-fidelity three-dimensional environment models are expensive to obtain, whereas geometric inaccuracies in low-fidelity models can alter the detected multipath components (MPCs) and consequently distort received-power and delay-domain twin channel statistics. Building on the DeepRT ray-tracing framework, this paper proposes DeepRT-Cal, a geometry-aware cross-fidelity calibration framework that predicts high-fidelity twin channel statistics from low-fidelity geometry and RT features.The network encodes global link descriptors, masked low-fidelity MPC tokens, propagation-corridor geometry, and link-centered environmental objects. During training, detailed geometry is introduced as privileged information with structured masking, while deployment requires only low-fidelity geometry and low-fidelity RT information. A link-conditioned cross-attention module retrieves the environmental context relevant to each Tx--Rx link. The prediction heads estimate high-fidelity twin channel statistics, including total received power, RMS delay spread, mean excess delay, and a normalized power-weighted power-delay profile (PDP). Outdoor evaluation shows that, in an non-line of sight (NLoS) region, the method reduces power MAE from 16.80 to 3.88 dB and RMS delay-spread MAE from 304.89 to 98.19 ns. In a LoS-dominated region, power prediction improves, while RMS delay-spread accuracy remains comparable to direct RT.

title: AISHELL8-FISHEYE: A Fisheye Audio-Visual Dataset for Target Speaker Extraction with Distortion-Aware Baselines
summary: Fisheye cameras offer wide visual coverage but distort facial and lip geometry, challenging audio-visual target speaker extraction. We introduce AISHELL8-FISHEYE, a 47.03-hour corpus of 94 Mandarin speakers with synchronized audio and paired fisheye and normal-camera videos. Speaker-disjoint splits and synthetic two-speaker mixtures support reproducible evaluation under matched acoustic conditions. We also establish a baseline that combines a lip-reading encoder with a frozen distortion-aware branch transferred from fisheye head pose estimation. On fisheye video, adding this branch to an adapted lip encoder improves scale-invariant signal-to-distortion ratio improvement from 10.47 to 11.84 dB. The branch does not improve performance with a frozen lip encoder, highlighting the importance of visual adaptation. A substantial gap to paired normal-camera inputs remains. The corpus and baseline resources support further research on speech extraction from distorted visual cues.

title: DNN-Driven Proactive UAV Trajectory and Beam Steering for Blockage-Resilient Communications
summary: This paper proposes Autonomous UAV Communication (AutUAVCom), a proactive communication system that jointly adapts the flight trajectory and RF beam steering to minimize UAV energy consumption while satisfying secrecy and reliability requirements for rescue teams operating in dynamic, cluttered, and GPS-denied environments. Unlike existing modelbased proactive approaches, AutUAVCom employs a deep neural network-based Tracking and Prediction (T&P) module that combines onboard sensing with spatiotemporal and body-orientation information to track users, localize blocking objects, and predict future trajectories and potential beam blockages. Building on the T&P module, we formulate a constrained optimization problem and develop a two-step iterative numerical approach. Monte Carlo simulations show that, relative to a reactive system, AutUAVCom achieves 10% and 19% gains in energy efficiency and channel secrecy, respectively, while reducing the outage probability by 85%, under a mean blockage arrival interval of 120 seconds and a mean blockage duration of 20 seconds.

title: Beyond the Pseudo-Inverse: GIM Precoding for Per-Antenna Power Minimisation in MU-MIMO
summary: We study linear precoder design for multi-user MIMO downlink under per-antenna power constraints (PAPC), which arise naturally when each antenna port has its own power amplifier. While the Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse is the unique optimal generalized inverse for zero-forcing precoding under a total power constraint [1], we prove this optimality does not extend to the MMSE/RZF case under PAPC. Any precoder in the Generalized Inverse Matrix (GIM) family shares the same effective channel and per-user SINRs as the pseudo-inverse baseline, while its null-space component reshapes the per-antenna power profile. This separation principle enables minimising peak per-antenna power at fixed SINR targets with zero SINR penalty. We characterise the convex peak-power problem over this family and its active-set optimality, establish MRT and ZF asymptotic limits, and provide a convergent first-order subgradient algorithm. Simulations with 8-64 antennas confirm gains of 1.9-3.7 dB over pseudo-inverse RZF, with GIM-MMSE eliminating essentially all PAPC violations up to 20% per-antenna budget imbalance. The framework applies directly to fully-digital massive MIMO. Cell-free and hybrid analog-digital arrays are promising extensions.

title: Pinching Antenna Systems (PASS) for Air-Ground Integrated Sensing and Communications (ISAC)
summary: This paper proposes a multi-user single-target air-ground integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) system, in which a ground pinching-antenna system (PASS) transmits communication and sensing signals and an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) receives the target echo. The communication and sensing beamforming vectors, pinching antenna positions, and UAV position are jointly optimized to minimize the weighted Cramér-Rao bound (CRB). A penalty dual decomposition (PDD) algorithm is developed for the resulting nonconvex problem. The auxiliary variable and beamforming subproblems admit globally optimal solutions in semi-closed form, while the positions of the pinching antennas and the UAV are updated by successive convex approximation (SCA). Under mild conditions, every accumulation point of the sequence generated by our proposed algorithm is a Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) point of the reformulated problem. Numerical results show that the proposed PASS-UAV design achieves a lower weighted CRB than conventional multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) and PASS benchmarks.

title: A Hybrid Digital/Analog Polyphase Filtering Approach for High-Speed RF-DACs
summary: This paper proposes a hybrid polyphase interpolation for RF-DACs that removes the need for full-rate digital commutation by using passive combining on the RF-DAC itself. A P-branch polyphase FIR filter is factored into M streams, each formed by a (P/M)-way digital commutator at fRF/M and driving a dedicated RF-DAC slice, giving either partial digital (1<M<P) or fully analog (M=P) recombination. We show that the slice array acts as a single full-rate DAC with an M-times longer zero-order hold, derive yield laws for slice gain, timing and unit-capacitor mismatch, and find that with retiming the binding requirement is sub-picosecond matching of the fRF clock arrival, so the best choice is the smallest M that closes digital timing. Two 28-nm digital macros, designed for a 12.8GSps output rate and verified by post-layout simulation, illustrate a 4-phase variant that closes timing up to 14.4GSps with its digital logic at fRF/4 and an 8-phase variant that closes timing up to 16GSps with its digital logic at fRF/8. The analog recombination is evaluated with a behavioral model of the slice array. The architectures target wideband software defined radio (SDR) platforms, including cognitive radio, electronic warfare, and satellite communications.

title: Sparse Array-Inspired Frame Structure Design for 5G NR ISAC
summary: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) has emerged as a promising paradigm for future wireless networks. However, the extensive occupation of time-frequency resources for sensing limits the communication capacity. To address the resource conflict, this paper proposes a novel sparse sensing frame structure aligned with the 5G new radio (5G NR) resource grid at the slot and physical resource block (PRB) levels through a predefined sensing-pattern block. Specifically, inspired by the design of two-dimensional (2D) sparse antenna arrays, we map the sparse spatial geometries onto the time-frequency resource grid. By leveraging the hole-free property of the difference coarray, we eliminate the range-velocity ambiguity and cast the sensing signals into a reconstructed higher-order tensor representation. For efficient parameter estimation, we propose a novel binary-tree-based tensor train decomposition (BT-TTD) algorithm that extracts lower-dimensional tensor train cores (TT-cores) and executes a Vandermonde-prior-guided rectified alternating least squares (RecALS) algorithm. Simulation results validate that the proposed scheme achieves competitive estimation accuracy with reduced complexity. Furthermore, we investigate the topological properties of various sparse patterns, revealing the inherent trade-off among sensing accuracy, resource occupancy, and computational complexity.

title: Expert Spindles in the Wild: Enriched Supervision for a Dense Detector
comments: 5 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Submitted to IEEE ISBI 2027 (under review)
summary: Sleep spindles are a hallmark of healthy NREM sleep whose frequency, amplitude, density, duration and topography vary with brain maturation, age and disease. Their manual annotation is impractical and variable between scorers, yet the public references used to train automatic detectors cover these characteristics only partially: stage N2 only, a single central derivation, or short pre-selected segments. Measuring duration and density requires dense detectors that learn event boundaries from annotated onsets and offsets, and therefore inherit the protocol under which those boundaries were scored. We introduce Expert Spindles in the Wild (ESW), a stage-agnostic expert spindle annotation set covering 19 complete MASS-SS2 recordings ($\approx$150 h of continuous EEG, 29,819 events). A sleep neurophysiologist annotated the recordings using the full EEG montage, blinded to sleep-stage labels and prior spindle annotations. On the 15 nights shared with historical scorers, ESW recovers 92.7% of E1 and 73.7% of E2 events, while recovering 81.6% of the MODA expert-consensus events on the common excerpts. Despite stage-blind annotation, 99.0% of ESW events occur in N2/N3. Used to train a fixed dense detector on a frozen SleepFM encoder, ESW reaches an event-level $F_1$ of 0.680 on 166 unseen MODA subjects, compared with 0.635 for E2 ($ΔF_1$ = +0.045, paired-bootstrap 95% CI [0.024, 0.065]). ESW is thus useful supervision for cross-dataset detection, and closer annotation-level agreement with the MODA consensus did not translate into better transfer performance in this experiment. The annotations are released under the MASS data-use terms (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23894975).
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Submitted to IEEE ISBI 2027 (under review)

title: Multi-Mode Pinching-Antenna-Based OFDM Systems: A Robust Design Perspective
summary: A robust transmission framework is proposed for a multi-mode pinching-antenna (MPA)-based orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) system under both channel state information (CSI) errors and PA positioning errors. A physical model is first developed based on the multi-mode coupled-mode equations (CMEs), which characterizes the frequency-dependent guided-mode propagation and the coupling among guided modes and PAs over the OFDM band. Based on this model, a worst-case sum-rate maximization problem is formulated to jointly optimize the baseband beamformer and the intended PA positions under CSI and PA positioning errors, subject to user quality-of-service (QoS) and transmit-power constraints. To solve the resulting non convex problem, the worst-case CSI is exactly obtained for any given PA positions by solving trust-region subproblems, while the PA positioning errors are handled by grid-based and second-order approximation-based scenario constructions. Then, an alternating optimization (AO) algorithm is developed, where the baseband beamformer and the intended PA positions are updated via the weighted minimum mean-square error (WMMSE) method and successive convex approximation (SCA), respectively. Both subproblems are solved efficiently by exploiting the Karush--Kuhn--Tucker (KKT) conditions. Numerical results show that the proposed robust design outperforms the non-robust and conventional robust benchmarks with the same multi-mode architecture in terms of both worst-case sum rate and QoS satisfaction. They also demonstrate that the proposed robust design satisfies the QoS requirements of all users more reliably than the baselines that consider either CSI errors or PA positioning errors.

title: Payload-Blind Bistatic Delay-Doppler Sensing with Phase-Injected Chirps in CE-OFDM
summary: Constant-envelope orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (CE-OFDM) preserves a unit-magnitude sample envelope, but its Hermitian-symmetric structure makes dedicated sensing pilots costly, and additive pilots disrupt this envelope. We show that injecting a known chirp, here a Zadoff-Chu (ZC) sequence, into the CE-OFDM phase enables payload-blind bistatic delay-Doppler sensing without dedicated sensing frames or an explicit pilot power split: the residual carrier, given by the ensemble mean under the adopted payload model, becomes an implicit superimposed pilot for a receive-only node. A Doppler-aligned receiver integrates this reference coherently across frames while the payload residual averages down. In contrast, phase-domain injected training (PIT) frame averaging, designed for quasi-static channel estimation, loses about 32 dB for the simulated target with 16 averaged frames. Closed-form approximations characterize the payload-induced floor, known-cell detection probability and direct-path tolerance. In the noise-limited simulations, the receiver incurs a 2.8 dB detection gap relative to a payload-aware matched filter without interference cancellation and matches a dedicated-pilot benchmark of equal reference energy without its 53% frame overhead.

title: Tomographic Sparse View Selection using the View Covariance Loss
comments: Accepted version of the article published in IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence. 11 pages main paper plus 3 pages supplementary material
summary: Standard computed tomography (CT) reconstruction algorithms such as filtered back projection (FBP) and Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) require many views for producing high-quality reconstructions, which can slow image acquisition and increase cost in non-destructive evaluation (NDE) applications. Over the past 20 years, a variety of methods have been developed for computing high-quality CT reconstructions from sparse views. However, the problem of how to select the best views for CT reconstruction remains open. In this paper, we present a novel view covariance loss (VCL) function that measures the joint information of a set of views by approximating the normalized mean squared error (NMSE) of the reconstruction. We present fast algorithms for computing the VCL along with an algorithm for selecting a subset of views that approximately minimizes its value. Our experiments on simulated and measured data indicate that for a fixed number of views our proposed view covariance loss selection (VCLS) algorithm results in reconstructions with lower NRMSE, fewer artifacts, and greater accuracy than current alternative approaches.
comment: Accepted version of the article published in IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence. 11 pages main paper plus 3 pages supplementary material

title: On PMU Adequacy for Wideband Dynamics Tracking Beyond Attenuation Assumptions
summary: Recent work highlights the inadequacy of standard synchrophasors in capturing high-frequency grid dynamics, including data center oscillations, primarily due to filtering and windowing attenuation during phasor estimation. This letter shows how synchrophasor ambient data spectrum itself contains information on attenuation, which provides a way to identify critically impacted measurements and potentially estimate and undo the effect. Results are shown for synthetic data as well as actual synchrophasor estimates from digital fault recorders (DFRs) within the Dominion Energy system.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Classical Communications for DPMZM-based NG-PON2 Systems
summary: This paper presents a framework for integrating quantum detection techniques into a Dual-Parallel Mach-Zehnder Modulator (DPMZM)-based Next Generation Passive Optical Network 2 (NG-PON2) communication system. We present a system model for the DPMZM-based NG-PON2 quantum communication system and characterize its signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), demonstrating its superiority over conventional MZM-based systems. We analyze the performance of various quantum modulation techniques, including binary phase-shift keying, quadrature phase-shift keying, and M-ary quadrature amplitude modulation. A comprehensive analytical framework is developed to evaluate the SNR, BER, and mutual information for both classical and quantum detection schemes within the DPMZM-based NG-PON2 quantum communication system. Our simulation results show that quantum detection significantly outperforms classical detection, and the DPMZM architecture further enhances the performance over the baseline MZM architecture by improving the effective modulation efficiency and receiver sensitivity.

title: A Tutorial on Practical QKD Post-Processing Algorithms Using a GUI-Based Simulation Framework
comments: Submitted to IEEE Open Journal of the Communications Society
summary: Recent experimental demonstrations of Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) have attracted significant attention for their ability to establish information-theoretically secure encryption keys for next-generation communication systems. As practical deployment accelerates, the realization of compact, scalable, and high-throughput discrete-variable (DV) QKD systems has become increasingly important. While advances in photonic integration are enabling low-size, low-weight, and low-power QKD hardware, the security and performance of these systems rely heavily on efficient post-processing techniques to generate identical, secure keys. This tutorial presents a comprehensive algorithm-level review of practical post-processing techniques for DV-QKD, with particular emphasis on information reconciliation methods based on Cascade, Winnow, low-density parity-check (LDPC), and polar codes. We also analyze the theoretical asymptotic and finite-size secret key rates (SKRs) of DV-QKD and benchmark these bounds against the practical SKRs achieved using actual post-processing algorithms. Furthermore, we present a server-client model to implement the entire QKD post-processing pipeline. The performance is evaluated in terms of QBER and SKR across various system parameters, considering the complete post-processing pipeline, including sifting, information reconciliation, privacy amplification, and authentication. This tutorial also presents a graphical user interface (GUI) for the QKD post-processing methods, enabling researchers, industry practitioners, and academic users to visualize and analyze the impact of different post-processing techniques and system parameters, such as QBER, on the SKR performance of DV-QKD systems.
comment: Submitted to IEEE Open Journal of the Communications Society

title: A Phase-Balanced Differential Rydberg-Atom Quantum Receiver for Weak GNSS Signal Detection
comments: 6 pages, 10 figures, submitted to IEEE ICC 2027 (in review)
summary: This paper proposes a phase-balanced differential Rydberg atomic quantum receiver (DRAQR) for weak-signal recovery, using local-oscillator phase control to reinforce differential signal responses and a shared squeezed-reservoir model to correlate inter-cell quantum projection noise (QPN) and photon shot noise (PSN). An analytical model incorporating QPN, PSN, intrinsic thermal noise (ITN), and inter-cell correlations quantifies signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) gain, outage-constrained minimum detectable power, and bit-error rate (BER) for square $M$-QAM. For the evaluated settings, SNR gain reaches approximately $10$~dB as PSN correlation approaches unity, with BER decreasing as correlation increases. Under Rician fading, at a $0$-dB threshold SNR and maximum outage probability of $0.1$, the minimum detectable power decreases from $-146.95$~dBm at $K=1.155$ to $-159.98$~dBm at $K=2.4$. Analytical results are validated against Monte-Carlo simulations over $150{,}000$ data runs per point for receiver-performance plots.
comment: 6 pages, 10 figures, submitted to IEEE ICC 2027 (in review)

title: A Unified Multisensor Machine-Learning Framework for Live Fuel Moisture Content Retrieval
comments: Published version in Remote Sensing (MDPI). Revised following re-submission to MDPI and peer review; supersedes the original preprint. 45 pages, 10 figures
summary: Live fuel moisture content controls vegetation flammability and is a high-importance variable in fire management. Nevertheless, it remains difficult to estimate and map over large areas due to the concentration of field observations in specific regions. We develop a unified machine-learning framework that estimates live fuel moisture content from satellite vegetation indices, meteorological variables, topography and seasonal predictors. GlobeLFMC 2.0 measurements are matched to Terra and Aqua MODIS, VIIRS, Landsat 8/9, Sentinel-2 and Sentinel-3 surface-reflectance products, combining the long MODIS record with finer-resolution recent observations. To account for differences among sensors, optical predictors are restricted to a common red, near-infrared and shortwave-infrared feature space; site--product combinations and field time series are screened for remote-sensing suitability; and spectral response function diagnostics are combined with target-independent empirical reflectance calibration toward a Sentinel-2 reference domain. Preliminary single-product experiments show that weather, topography and cyclic day-of-year provide most of the predictive gain beyond vegetation indices, whereas optional product-specific predictors do not justify their additional dependencies. Separate Grass, Shrub and Tree models are trained with Random Forest and XGBoost regressors. Under the primary validation design, which withholds observation dates from sites represented in training, the best models achieve pooled R2 values of 0.715, 0.693 and 0.700 for Grass, Shrub and Tree, respectively. The framework can incorporate additional optical sensors when compatible reflectance bands, documented spectral responses and sufficient overlap observations are available for calibration and validation.
